entry.title: Wigan crush Leeds to move closer to winning shield
entry.body: Wigan crush Leeds to move closer to winning shield - Published Betfred Super League Leeds (8) 8 Tries: Handley Goals: Connor 2 Wigan (16) 40 Tries: Keighran 3, Daniel, Marshall, French, Field Goals: Keighran 6 Wigan Warriors produced an outstanding display on the big occasion once again as they defeated Leeds Rhinos to take a giant step towards lifting the League Leaders' Shield. The Warriors leapfrogged the Rhinos to move two points clear at the top and if they match Leeds' result in the final game of the regular season on Friday, they will claim their second piece of silverware of the year. It was their 14th straight Super League win and it is hard to imagine them not beating Catalans Dragons at home to finish the job, with the Rhinos welcoming Hull FC at the same time. Two early tries from Adam Keighran put them in charge at a sold-out Headingley before Ash Handley got Leeds on the scoreboard before the break. Teenage winger Austin Daniel scored only his second Super League try to restore a 10-point advantage before fellow winger Liam Marshall crossed early in the second half to put Wigan firmly in control. Their defence remained resolute as Leeds tried to get back into the game, and further tries from star backs Bevan French and Jai Field and a hat-trick from Keighran showed why they will be strong favourites to win the Grand Final at Old Trafford on 3 October. - Wakefield stay in top-four hunt with win over Wire - Published5 hours ago - York run in five tries for dream win over Catalans - Published2 hours ago - Women's Super League: Wigan thrash Leeds to storm on - Published3 hours ago The Rhinos have been top since May in pursuit of their first silverware since 2020 â a long wait for one of rugby league's powerhouses - while they have not finished top of Super League since 2015. But the Warriors have been in their rearview mirror as they have been imperious through the summer, on the back of a winning streak which started more than three months ago with a dismantling of Hull KR in the Challenge Cup final at Wembley. After a shaky spring, Wigan have been back to their best as they chase a treble, to go with the quadruple they secured two years ago. Super League's leading try scorer, Maika Sivo, did not make the Leeds squad after recovering from a broken arm, but there was a setback for the hosts early in the game as full-back Lachie Miller limped off with a hamstring injury. With the Rhinos reshuffling, Wigan pounced as the great teams do. Sharp handling from French and Keighran got the ball to teenage winger Austin Daniel who, on just his fourth league appearance, showed a turn of pace down the wing and then awareness to set up Keighran to score. Oliver Partington had a try disallowed, but the Warriors were not to be denied as French's bullet pass put fellow Australian Keighran over again. Leeds were stunned but found a response as Connor hoisted a high kick which was brilliantly caught and then touched down by captain Handley. They were right back in the contest, but French simply dipped into his box of tricks to move Wigan further clear as the stand-off threw a sensational pass that took out three defenders and gave Daniel a walk-in. Connor kicked a goal on the stroke of half-time to reduce the gap to eight points. But the visitors claimed the first score of the second half through Marshall's trademark finish in the left corner, although the unhappy hosts believed Wigan had knocked on in the build-up. There was a hint of desperation as Leeds tried to force their way back into the game, but there were no chinks in the Warriors defence and their class was on show at the other end. Harry Smith's clever kick found space and French, on his 200th career appearance, was first on to it, before Field's dazzling feet grabbed Wigan's sixth try. Keighran then completed his hat-trick as the clock was ticking down to cap another glorious night for this storied club. 'We let the club down' - reaction Leeds Rhinos head coach Brad Arthur told BBC Radio Leeds: "We're disappointed, we didn't put our best foot forward tonight. It was a big occasion for the club and not through effort, but we let ourselves down and we let the club down. "It's certainly not over, but we've got to dust ourselves down. We've got a big game next week and we need to regain some form. On Lachlan Miller's injury: "It's not great. He's obviously got to go and have scans, but I think he's torn his hamstring. We'll have to wait and see. "It's hard to replace a player of his quality, but then it's hard to replace a full-back, they're so integral to your defensive line, the organisation of that and how he returns the ball. "We were a bit disjointed from it, but we've got to be a bit more resilient." Leeds: Miller; Hall, Bird, Handley, Newman; Croft, Connor; Oledzki, O'Connor, Jenkins, Watkins, Hankinson, Cassell. Interchanges: C Smith, Lodge, Lloyd, Holroyd. Wigan: Field; Daniel, Keighran, Eckersley, Marhsall; French, H Smith; Havard, O'Neill, Thompson, McDermott, Partington, Ellis. Interchanges: Nsemba, Walters, Mago, Kerr.
entry.summary: Wigan Warriors move within touching distance of winning the League Leaders' Shield after a superb victory at closest rivals Leeds Rhinos.

entry.title: Robert Pattinson Kisses Suki Waterhouse as ‘Primetime’ Rocks Venice With 7-Minute Standing Ovation - Variety
entry.body: “Primetime,” a thriller starring Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, made its debut at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday to an enthusiastic seven-minute ovation. Venice went fully in for Pattinson’s immersive performance as Hansen, the “Dateline” journalist and host who sets out to make television history with “To Catch a Predator.” And one of the biggest fans in attendance? Pattinson’s partner Suki Waterhouse, who cheered perhaps loudest during the seven-minute standing ovation and leaned forward and kissed Pattinson on the lips as the crowd applauded his tour-de-force performance. (In Venice, actors are seated in the front row of the balcony and their partners must sit a row behind them.) As the ovation stretched into its sixth minute, the audience began chanting for director Lance Oppenheim and singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers, who makes her acting debut in the film. Skyler Gisondo and Merritt Wever also star. Based on Luke Dittrich’s 2007 Esquire article “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die,” “Primetime” follows the production of the popular series, in which Hansen attempted to confront child sexual predators in complex sting operations. Popular on Variety Massive crowds outside the Palazzo del Cinema were chanting “Robert! Robert!” as they baked in the sun on a brutally hot Saturday afternoon. Pattinson, Gisando and Bridgers dutifully signed autographs and posed for tons of selfies with fans while Waterhouse made small talk with producers off to the side of the action. Pattinson dabbed the sweat off his forehead with napkins before posing for a cast photo. Former NBC chief Jeff Zucker, who appears in the movie as himself, also walked the red carpet, as did producer Ari Aster. “Primetime” marks Oppenheim’s feature debut, having previously helmed acclaimed documentaries such as “Some Kind of Heaven” and HBO’s “Ren Faire.” A24 will release “Primetime” in theaters on Sept. Hansen has been vocal in his criticisms about “Primetime,” saying he wasn’t involved in the creative process and hadn’t seen the movie. He called Pattinson’s portrayal “overly dramatic” and questioned the studio’s “motive” in dramatizing the making of the hit reality series. Hansen has also stressed that “Primetime” isn’t a literal account of his career and that he wasn’t consulted during the making of the movie. “He’s saying things I never said and doing things I never did, and that’s not who I am. I’m a nice guy, except when it comes to criminals and predators,” Hansen previously said. “I think people should remember that it is a work of fiction, only based on real-life events.” At a press conference earlier on Saturday, Pattinson suggested that Hansen could come around once he sees the film. “Obviously, I hope he likes the movie,” Pattinson said. “There’s something electrifying about him. I would hope the amount of inspiration his character has given a lot of people for years is some kind of compliment.” “Primetime” continues a banner year for Pattinson, who stars in such high-profile films as this spring’s indie hit “The Drama,” Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster “The Odyssey” and Denis Villeneuve’s upcoming tentpole “Dune: Part III.” And Pattinson’s schedule remains packed: He jetted to Lido from London, where he is currently filming “The Batman: Part II,” reprising his role as reclusive billionaire-turned-vigilante Bruce Wayne. “When you get the momentum going, it’s strangely not that hard,” Pattinson said at the presser. Plus, he joked, “I just had a baby. I had no desire to go out at night. So suddenly I had twice as much time, which was helpful.”
entry.summary: Robert Pattinson Kisses Suki Waterhouse as ‘Primetime’ Rocks Venice With 7-Minute Standing Ovation Variety Primetime review: Robert Pattinson is extraordinary as controversial paedophile-hunter Chris Hansen ★★★★★ BBC In ‘Primetime,’ Robert Pattinson takes on the ‘irresistible’ role of Chris Hansen AP News Robert Pattinson Won’t Be the Only ‘Primetime’ Star to Generate Oscar Buzz IndieWire 'Primetime' Review: Robert Pattinson's Uncanny Portrait of Predation Variety

entry.title: ‘Evil Dead’ Star Bruce Campbell Says He Has 5 Years to Live After Incurable Cancer Diagnosis: I’m ‘Dying’ but ‘I’m Moving On’
entry.body: “Evil Dead” star Bruce Campbell is opening up about his battle with cancer, revealing that he’s been given about five years to live. Back in March, Campbell revealed he had been diagnosed with a cancer that was “treatable but not curable.” “These days, when someone is having a health issue, it’s referred to as an ‘opportunity,’ so let’s go with that — I’m having one of those,” he wrote on X in March. “It’s also called a type of cancer that’s ‘treatable’ not ‘curable.’ I apologize if that’s a shock – it was to me too.” Campbell didn’t go into detail about what type of cancer he’d been diagnosed with, but wrote that “professionally, a few things will have to change. Appearances and cons and work in general need to take back seat to treatment. My plan is to get as well as I possibly can over the summer so that I can tour with my new movie ‘Ernie & Emma’ this fall.” Popular on Variety On Wednesday’s episode of “The Adam Carolla Show,” Campbell opened up more about his diagnosis and treatment while also discussing his new movie. “I’m in a five-year prognosis,” he said. “With the type of cancer that I have, which I don’t want to get into, the current thing is a five-year deal.” When Carolla asked if that meant Campbell had five years to live, the actor replied “give or take.” “It’s a fascinating thing that takes place because [cancer] messes with your head, too. I’ve decided though, pretty specifically, to live with it, not die from it,” he added. “You can go down a massive rabbit hole. The cancer rabbit hole is enormous. You can go into focus groups of 10,000 guys who have exactly what you have. I won’t touch it with a 10-foot pole.” Campbell serves as director, writer, producer and lead actor in “Ernie & Emma,” in which he plays a widower scattering his late wife’s ashes, reflecting on their relationship together and confronting his grief. “It’s a very fascinating time of having a movie about a guy who’s spreading his wife’s ashes, who died, made by a guy who’s dying,” he told Carolla. Campbell, who starred as the chainsaw-wielding Ash Williams in director Sam Raimi’s original “Evil Dead” trilogy, executive produced this summer’s installment in the horror franchise, “Evil Dead Burn.” He’s also an EP on the next movie, 2028’s “Evil Dead Wrath.” “I’m moving on. I got a movie to promote. And when I promote this movie, I have nothing. I’m free and clear when I promote this movie mentally,” Campbell said. “You have to make this decision of, ‘Well, OK, but do I have to stop everything that I’m doing because of this?’ Well, no.” Watch his full interview below.

entry.title: Andrew Scott Has Waited His Whole Career for a Role Like ‘Elsinore.’ Can Focus and the Bard Anoint Him With an Oscar?
entry.body: Andrew Scott is the prince of Telluride. There are performances that feel like a reckoning, and performances that feel like a resurrection. Andrew Scott’s work in “Elsinore,” which had its world premiere Friday night at the Telluride Film Festival, is somehow both — a great actor playing a great actor as the curtain starts to fall, and refusing to let it. Directed by Simon Stone and written by Stephen Beresford, “Elsinore” tells the true story of Ian Charleson, the Scottish “Chariots of Fire” star who spent the last year of his life playing Hamlet at London’s National Theatre as AIDS was quietly taking his life. He died in 1990 at 40. His Hamlet — hailed then as one of the finest of its generation — became a farewell disguised as a role. The casting is too perfect to be accidental. Scott is himself a celebrated London Hamlet, here playing a man whose Hamlet was his last act of defiance. “Elsinore” is, at its heart, a love letter to actors — to the craft as vocation, to the courage of standing in the light when the body is failing. And a milestone waits inside the role. No openly gay man has ever won the Oscar for best actor, and Scott could very well become the first. Popular on Variety Make no mistake, this is the role of Scott’s career and it lands him toward the forefront of a best actor conversation he has been circling for years. He has never been Oscar-nominated — a fact that curdled into open disdain when the Academy passed over his shattering turn in “All of Us Strangers.” “Elsinore” is the correction: he captures Charleson’s wit, vanity, terror and grace inside the same breath and in the final stretch, he nails Hamlet’s readiness measured against a dying man’s own — the sustained high-wire work voters still see behind their eyes in January. It’s also a role the Academy has never resisted. Voters are reliably moved by the actor staring down the barrel of death — Tom Hanks in “Philadelphia” (1993), Matthew McConaughey in “Dallas Buyers Club” (2013) and Anthony Hopkins vanishing into dementia in “The Father” (2020). “Elsinore” hands Scott the AIDS-era variation, with the added charge of real history — a story to discover even for those who think they already know it. Charleson was a real man and a real actor, dying as he did, playing Hamlet as he did. That is not a fact that asks for votes so much as one that issues a commandment, and I dare any Academy member not to see the worth in honoring such a life through a vessel as gifted as Scott. Then there is Olivia Colman, who has entered her “Maggie Smith” era and is plainly having the time of her life. Her supporting turn as Charleson’s doctor is all steel and mischief — grumpy one moment, gutting the next — the work of a past winner (“The Favourite”) who keeps finding registers no one knew she had. It belongs in the supporting actress conversation without an asterisk, the season’s most quotable grande dame showcase since Smith herself. Watch, too, for Billie Piper, as a casting director and Charleson’s confidant, who does the quietest and maybe the most surprising work in the film. Stone directed her to an Olivier Award in his radical stage “Yerma,” and their reunion could carry her into a film-awards conversation for the first time. If Focus campaigns her with nerve, she’s a supporting actress spoiler nobody is clocking just yet. The rest of the craft work is impeccable. Stefan Gregory’s score rips — propulsive where you brace for a sonorous monologue, tender where you expect something loud. Stone directs with a theater maker’s reverence for the actor’s face; Beresford, who wrote “Pride,” has built a script funnier than any logline would suggest and gutting exactly when it must be. One curious wrinkle: the script credit reads “based on an idea by Ethan Silverman,” which raises the kind of question pundits love — a “Barbie”-style scramble over whether the Academy files it as original or adapted. The WGA has designated it original. What ultimately matters is this: is it Scott only, or should we brace for more? A lead performance, fully embraced, can drag a whole film up the ballot. Sandra Bullock’s “The Blind Side” was beloved enough to pull the movie into best picture — its only other nomination — and she won. “Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close” managed the same trick, riding supporting actor nominee Max von Sydow to a best picture berth; it won neither, but von Sydow was plainly the runner-up to Christopher Plummer’s winning turn in “Beginners” — itself that film’s only nomination. Then there are the critically adored turns that stand alone. Colin Firth in Tom Ford’s “A Single Man” managed exactly one nomination — his — and lost. A year later, folded inside the 12-nomination embrace of “The King’s Speech,” he walked away with the prize. A lone acting nod is a precarious perch, and Scott will need more than that to convert his into a trophy. “Elsinore” likely needs Colman and Piper in supporting, Beresford’s screenplay on the ballot — or perhaps techs like makeup and editing — and even a best picture berth. A great performance gets you nominated; a film full of them gets you onstage. This can be Focus Features’ specialty. No specialty distributor has been better over the last 25 years at minting best actor winners from biopics — Adrien Brody (“The Pianist”), Sean Penn (“Milk”), Matthew McConaughey (“Dallas Buyers Club”), Eddie Redmayne (“The Theory of Everything”) and Gary Oldman (“Darkest Hour”) — five men, each playing a real one, each launched off a fall-festival bow and a patient platform release. And every one of those films was a best picture nominee. “Elsinore” follows the blueprint to the letter. The material carries its own Oscar pedigree — and Focus is riding it. Last winter the studio won its first best actress Oscar with Jessie Buckley in “Hamnet,” the story of the family loss that gave the world “Hamlet”; a few years earlier, Kenneth Branagh, cinema’s foremost Shakespearean, took original screenplay for the Focus release “Belfast.” The Academy’s affection reaches back further, to the wins “Shakespeare in Love” minted for Gwyneth Paltrow and Judi Dench. Now, two years running, the studio has a “Hamlet” in the race. The Bard has been good to this address. Hamlet’s final words are “the rest is silence.” “Elsinore,” and the actor at its center, make a beautiful liar of the line. On Friday night in the mountains, the rest was a room on its feet and an actor, at last, getting the reception for the role he was born to play. Read Variety’s review of “Elsinore” here.

entry.title: Hey, Oscars: No Sympathy Required to Give Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ the Consideration It Deserves
entry.body: Let’s dispense with the suspense. Mike Leigh has been nominated for an Academy Award seven times and has won it zero times. He has a Palme d’Or, a Golden Lion, five decades of films that taught generations of actors what unglamorous truth looks like and one of the most distinctive bodies of work in modern British cinema. What he does not have is an Oscar — and based on the reviews and reactions out of the Telluride Film Festival, where the film bowed Friday night, it’s about damn time he got one. “Tender Loving Care” arrives carrying the weight none of Leigh’s previous films did. At 83, and contending with myosotis, a muscle-wasting condition that kept him from his own Telluride premiere, Leigh has said this is most likely his last film. Bleecker Street opens it Dec. 4 after a fall festival run the industry reserves for titles it takes seriously. Popular on Variety That makes the season’s obvious question unavoidable: What should the Academy do with Mike Leigh’s final film? The answer is not — give him an Oscar because he is 83. It is — watch the movie, and you’ll see why you’d want to. “Tender Loving Care” does not need a sympathy campaign. It is vintage Leigh — wry, melancholy, humane, alert to the small emotional humiliations that become, over the course of a life, the events that define us. Kate O’Flynn’s Amy anchors it — an Emmy nominee for “Widow’s Bay,” and when the trophies are handed out Sept. 14, very possibly a winner — a social worker steadying a father in decline, gutted by a breakup and kept upright by wine and by Rosie, the live-wire best friend played exquisitely by Alice Bailey Johnson. Marion Bailey, as Amy’s mother, has already emerged from Telluride as a standout, a veteran thespian never given her proper due. A film about the daily labor of caring for people, made by a filmmaker who has spent 50 years caring, without vanity, about the interior lives most movies never bother to notice. It’s a perfect bookend to a career — and it closes on perhaps the most haunting final shot of any film in a decade. There’s a smaller bookend folded inside it, too: Leigh gave O’Flynn her first job, on “Happy-Go-Lucky,” at 21. She returns for his last. That sets up a campaign with an unusual shape and real vigor. Leigh carries the legacy narrative, but the film has to prove first that the work is competitive in a year crowded with filmmakers nursing overdue stories of their own. So the cleanest argument for Leigh is historical, not sentimental. Seven nominations and zero wins is a remarkable record. Twice — for “Secrets & Lies” and “Vera Drake” — the Academy nominated Leigh for both writing and directing in the same year, the dual embrace it reserves for its favorites. It has honored him again and again without ever closing the final distance. This is not an artist who spent a career waiting for his first invitation. The performances could help carry him there. O’Flynn and Bailey have the most obvious pathways, though where their teams ultimately campaign is still being sorted — and pundits will argue over where the two should land, which is rarely where they actually do. When two women read as co-leads, the Academy has grown allergic to rewarding both in the same category: the last time it nominated two lead actresses from a single film was “Thelma & Louise,” Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis, in 1991. So I’d bet the campaign splits them — O’Flynn, the anchor, in lead actress and Bailey in supporting. It should be duly noted, Bailey Johnson would be a worthy option to join whichever lady decides on the supporting campaign and as the ailing father, Paul Jesson is also incredibly rich and dynamic and would be worthy of consideration. But Bleecker Street will have to decide where to spend. An intimate British drama cannot campaign on every front with the force of a studio tent-pole. That is where the festival strategy matters. Toronto should widen the critical and industry conversation. The New York Film Festival drops the film into the center of the American awards ecosystem. The distributor’s job now is turning that accumulation into industry votes. There is a trap in the “last film” framing, too. Leigh’s age and health explain the stakes of the moment, but they should never become the reason to vote. The Academy has a long, familiar habit of honoring artists after the fact. The more respectful campaign makes the case while the artist is still here — still working at full command of his gifts. This is not a plea for a career-achievement handout. It is simply an argument that the film should earn the consideration on its own merits, and that a body claiming to honor the year’s best would embarrass itself to overlook a master telling us, gently, that he is done. He named the film “Tender Loving Care.” The least the Academy can do is extend some.

entry.title: Dolly Parton's sister slams 'fake AI garbage' in the wake of icon's death - USA Today
entry.body: Dolly Parton's sister slams 'fake AI garbage' in the wake of icon's death Dolly Parton's sister Stella Parton is condemning the deluge of misinformation being spread in the wake of the country star's death. The younger Parton, 77, took time from her morning “coffee hour" Friday, Sept. 4, to express how such online negativity has taken an emotional toll on her family as they continue grieving the “I Will Always Love You” singer, who died Aug. In a two-slide statement on Instagram, Stella Parton first thanked the "genuine" supporters who have been kind and respectful during the Parton family's bereavement, then addressed the bad-faith social media users who have been anything but considerate. Stella Parton slams 'fake AI garbage' following Dolly Parton's death “Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers,” she wrote. “There is a tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted everyday and it’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore.” “As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move on to the next stampede of endless misinformation,” Stella Parton added, imploring fans to "show more compassion and wisdom as we move forward in life." Rather than indulge in "clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets" concerning the "Jolene" singer's death, Stella Parton urged fans to "use my sister's life as an example for tolerance and respect toward others." As a final point of advice, she reminded fans to remember this: "At the end of the day or the end of a life, how will you feel about yourself? It's not about what other individuals you will never meet think of you!" Stella Parton's message comes mere days after the "Steel Magnolias" actress' star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame was allegedly vandalized. (Her star has since been replaced and will reopen to the public Sept. 14.) Stella Parton remembers Dolly Parton, recalls icon's final days The "I Want to Hold You in My Dreams Tonight" singer has been outspoken about grieving her sister's loss. When the news broke, she released a heartfelt tribute to her big sister, recalling their Tuesday morning routine and the Queen of Country's final days. "What the world saw is exactly who she was, so much so, she told me recently that if there was no hope for her, she would still allow her medical team to try experimental drugs in the hope of helping others in the future," she wrote on Facebook. "My sister was always thinking of others and if you want to honor her legacy, show more kindness, lift others up and give more of your time and resources as she continued to do to the very end," she added. "Dolly loved the world and everyone in it." How did Dolly Parton die? Parton died aged 80 on Aug. 25, following a private cancer battle, her representatives confirmed to USA TODAY. The "9 to 5" star's death came 16 months after the loss of Dean, who died in March 2025 at age 82. Her nephew Bryan Seaver, who is the son of the singer's sister Cassie, delivered the news of her death via video announcement on social media, per her wishes. Her niece Lainey Mae Parton confirmed on social media that Parton had been laid to rest on Aug. 28 in a small and private memorial held for her immediate family.

entry.title: Telluride Toasts Andrew Haigh as ‘A Long Winter’ Hands Fred Hechinger and Caitríona Balfe Awards-Worthy Roles
entry.body: At one point, Haigh’s screenplay was set in Spain, where Tóibín’s story takes place in the Pyrenees. The finished film relocates the tale to the stark American West of the 1950s, where a family — anchored by Fred Hechinger, Caitríona Balfe, Ebon Moss-Bachrach and Kit Connor — braces for winter until the mother vanishes into a snowstorm and her son sets out to find her. Haigh has jokingly called the film his version of “The Revenant,” a wilderness passion project nearly two decades in the making. But beneath the joke is something more personal: an “endpoint,” as he has described it, for a run of films addressed to a younger, sadder version of himself. He also appeared ready for the exaction. “You’ll see the film and go, ‘What the fuck is he talking about?’” drawing laughter from the Telluride audience.

entry.title: Dramatic twist in harassment suit against star CBS correspondent Matt Gutman - New York Post
entry.body: Dramatic twist in harassment suit against star CBS correspondent Matt Gutman See more of our coverage in your search results. Add The California Post on Google CBS News star Matt Gutman is almost in the clear after a former coworker moved to have him dropped from a harassment suit filed against the correspondent and his former network. Lawyers for ex-ABC News producer Samira Said filed a request in LA Superior Court on Friday to drop Gutman from her wrongful termination lawsuit. Former ABC News staffer Samira Said had alleged that Gutman made sexualized comments during two assignments several years ago, naming him in a lawsuit filed against the network and its parent company, The Walt Disney Co., in Los Angeles Superior Court last month. It’s unclear why the decision was made to drop Gutman from the lawsuit. Gutman’s current network, CBS News, declined to comment Saturday. The California Post contacted the correspondent for comment. CBS News boss Bari Weiss hired Gutman shortly after taking the reins in October 2025. According to the initial suit, Said claimed Gutman began discussing and rating the appearance of a female correspondent while the two were on an assignment. Other male crew members allegedly joined the conversation and tried to get Said to weigh in. She refused and told them the discussion was inappropriate, according to the lawsuit. Said also alleged a second incident occurred while she and Gutman were covering a press event for a movie release. The two disagreed about whether they should leave the work site, the suit claimed, with Gutman allegedly responding with a “sexualized insinuation” about Said in front of several coworkers. Said alleged the comments were demeaning and “reduced [her] professional judgment to a sexualized stereotype.” She is still pursuing a wrongful termination lawsuit against ABC News and The Walt Disney Co. Said, who worked as an ABC News field producer for four years, claims she was wrongfully fired in 2025 after dealing with mental health issues. California Post App: Download here!

entry.title: Original ‘Practical Magic’ Star Alexandra Artrip Addresses ‘Negativity’ Over Recasting in Sequel: They ‘Did What They Thought Was Best to Be Successful’
entry.body: Alexandra Artrip, who played the youngest daughter of Sandra Bullock’s character Sally Owens in 1998’s “Practical Magic,” has weighed in on the sequel’s decision to recast her and fellow original actor Evan Rachel Wood in the upcoming sequel. Artrip played Antonia Owens alongside Wood as her older sister Kylie, but their roles were given to younger actresses Maisie Williams and Joey King, respectively, in “Practical Magic 2.” Wood spoke out about the recasting earlier in the week, saying that “no one who worked on the original movie” reached out to her. She said that she did hear from King, who took over her role as Kylie, and that she was a “sweetheart.” Artrip posted a video on Instagram and responded to comments criticizing the recastings. “I love hearing your stories and connections to the film, but I get comments like this a lot, and I see them going on a lot of content around the sequel,” Artrip said. “I think the sentiment is right, people are trying to show support for Evan and myself and the original film and everything it’s meant to so many people, but I just don’t want my stuff to be a space for negativity. Maisie and Joey are lovely actresses, and I’m sure the production team did what they thought was best for the film to be successful.” Popular on Variety She added, “I just think we should support the film, give it a shot, go in with an open mind. Nothing can take away from what the original film was, and I’m excited that we’re able to build on that world with a new novel, new content in 2026, and that it’s given me a space to revisit all those beloved memories all these years later.” “Practical Magic 2” director Susanne Bier also weighed in on the recastings, telling Variety at the premiere that it was “not personal.” “The kids in the story are right out of college, so it wasn’t really a question,” she said. “We had to recast and we had to get some kids that [had been out of college].” “Practical Magic 2” opens in theaters on Sept.

entry.title: Witkoff and Kushner meet with Putin about ending Ukraine war
entry.body: President Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin Saturday and discussed U.S. ideas for ending the war in Ukraine. Why it matters: Witkoff and Kushner want to resume direct talks between Russia and Ukraine after negotiations were suspended six months ago and the fighting has escalated ahead of winter. Witkoff and Kushner, who are expected to travel to Kyiv on Sunday, got Russia and Ukraine to agree to a short pause in airstrikes to allow the trip to take place. What they are saying: Putin told Witkoff and Kushner at the top of the three-hour meeting that he has "full trust" in the U.S. mediation between Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff thanked Putin for releasing ex-U.S. Marine Robert Gilman and for agreeing to pause airstrikes against Ukraine while U.S. negotiators are visiting Kyiv. Putin said the pause will begin at midnight Saturday Moscow time and noted that Ukraine also reduced its strikes. "We will do our utmost to provide for the safety of the negotiations," Putin said. Yes, but: Over the last several days, Russia dramatically increased its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine, including Kyiv and other major cities. The big picture: The trip to Kyiv by Trump's envoys will be the highest-level visit by a U.S. official to Ukraine since President Trump started his second term. If the U.S. government plane carrying Witkoff and Kushner touches down in Ukraine on Sunday, it will be the first international flight that lands in the country since the war started in February 2022.

entry.title: U.S. attacks 3 Iranian tankers in tit-for-tat response
entry.body: U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy warships, U.S. Central Command said. Why it matters: The strikes continue a tit-for-tat war that just passed the six-month mark . A U.S. official told Axios this week it had a new "tanker-for-tanker" policy approved by President Trump. Driving the news: CENTCOM said it retaliated after a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer evaded missiles fired by Iran. The U.S. attacks "permanently disabled" the M/T Downy and the M/T Stark 1, CENTCOM said in a news release. They also "completely destroyed" the M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman after the crew was warned to abandon ship. CENTCOM posted footage of the strikes on social media. The big picture: On the first day of the war, Trump told Axios he "can go long and take over the whole thing, or end it in two or three days." The next day, he predicted to the Daily Mail the military campaign would "take four weeks — or less." Six months later, the U.S. and Iran are still trading attacks. The latest exchange came a day after Trump called the Iran conflict "small potatoes" and two days after Vice President Vance insisted there was no war and "no active shooting" between the two. An Aug. 14–17 Economist/YouGov poll found 65% of Americans want the U.S. to make a deal to end the war as quickly as possible.

entry.title: Trump’s MAGA Inc. sends $10M to Texas in first general election spend of the year
entry.body: President Donald Trump’s super PAC is shelling out $10 million for Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign, its first general election contribution ahead of the November midterms, according to a filing made public Saturday. It’s a welcome sign for Republicans, who have implored the president to mobilize his massive campaign war chest and groused that he must be the one to pull Paxton — whom he helped to defeat popular incumbent John Cornyn in the GOP primary — over the line in Texas against state Rep. James Talarico. "High Tax Talarico wants to take money out of Texans' pockets, MAGA Inc. spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer said in a statement. "MAGA Inc. is going to ensure Texas knows about Talarico's radical policies and elects Ken Paxton to the U.S. Senate." A spokesperson for the Talarico campaign suggested the super PAC isn't telling the truth about the Democratic nominee. “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James Talarico because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system,” spokesperson JT Ennis said. Paxton's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In an Oval Office press conference Friday, Trump pledged to pour “probably $400, 500 million” into the midterms, telling reporters the super PAC had amassed “close to a billion dollars.” The $10 million unveiled Saturday is the only amount known to have been spent by MAGA Inc. so far this general election cycle. “We’re going to spend a lot of money because we don’t want to lose our country,” Trump said. “I’m going to spend whatever amount of money necessary to try to help us, and this is money from MAGA Inc. This is my money that I control.” But with Republicans locked in hyper-competitive Senate races in a series of battleground states, and the GOP poised to perhaps lose control of the House for the first time since January 2023, the super PAC had previously refrained from spending to defeat Democrats this fall. Money from MAGA Inc. had only recently started to trickle out to boost GOP candidates, most of whom faced competitive primaries. It spent more than $827,000 to boost Sen. Darline Graham in the primary runoff in August. The super PAC raised $3 million in July and $18 million in June . Before the spend to boost Graham, MAGA Inc. hadn’t spent on a candidate since May, when it doled out $560,000 to MAGA KY , which supported Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) challenger in that month’s primary. The super PAC isn’t directly controlled by the president or the White House, and super PACs are supposed to operate independently, but candidates, including Trump, often have significant sway over the organizations. Paxton is in the middle of a closer-than-expected race against Talarico in Texas, where Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 14 points in 2024. He faces a major funding disparity and has been dogged by a wide variety of scandals that have traditional donors looking the other way.
entry.summary: President Donald Trump’s super PAC is shelling out $10 million for Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign, its first general election contribution ahead of the November midterms, according to a filing made public Saturday. It’s a welcome sign for Republicans, who have implored the president to mobilize his massive campaign war chest and groused that he must be the one to pull Paxton — whom he helped to defeat popular incumbent John Cornyn in the GOP primary — over the line in Texas against state Rep. James Talarico. "High Tax Talarico wants to take money out of Texans' pockets, MAGA Inc. spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer said in a statement. "MAGA Inc. is going to ensure Texas knows about Talarico's radical policies and elects Ken Paxton to the U.S. Senate." A spokesperson for the Talarico campaign suggested the super PAC isn't telling the truth about the Democratic nominee. “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James Talarico because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system,” spokesperson JT Ennis said. Paxton's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In an Oval Office press conference Friday, Trump pledged to pour “probably $400, 500 million” into the midterms, telling reporters the super PAC had amassed “close to a billion dollars.” The $10 million unveiled Saturday is the only amount known to have been spent by MAGA Inc. so far this general election cycle. “We’re going to spend a lot of money because we don’t want to lose our country,” Trump said. “I’m going to spend whatever amount of money necessary to try to help us, and this is money from MAGA Inc. This is my money that I control.” But with Republicans locked in hyper-competitive Senate races in a series of battleground states, and the GOP poised to perhaps lose control of the House for the first time since January 2023, the super PAC had previously refrained from spending to defeat Democrats this fall. Money from MAGA Inc. had only recently started to trickle out to boost GOP candidates, most of whom faced competitive primaries. It spent more than $827,000 to boost Sen. Darline Graham in the primary runoff in August. The super PAC raised $3 million in July and $18 million in June . Before the spend to boost Graham, MAGA Inc. hadn’t spent on a candidate since May, when it doled out $560,000 to MAGA KY , which supported Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) challenger in that month’s primary. The super PAC isn’t directly controlled by the president or the White House, and super PACs are supposed to operate independently, but candidates, including Trump, often have significant sway over the organizations. Paxton is in the middle of a closer-than-expected race against Talarico in Texas, where Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 14 points in 2024. He faces a major funding disparity and has been dogged by a wide variety of scandals that have traditional donors looking the other way.

entry.title: "We're stuck:" GOP accepts Trump's all-about-me midterms
entry.body: President Trump is hitting the campaign trail and doing the last thing many Republicans want: making the 59 days to the Nov. 3 midterms a referendum on him. At the same time, they know it's inevitable. Why it matters : Most Republicans are too scared to bluntly tell Trump how unpopular he is. And Trump wants an unprecedented convention next week, ads and events to focus on him. The big picture : Their timidity aside, Republicans need Trump's low-propensity voters to turn out. So they're going along with a Trump-focused strategy that many believe could cost them credibility — along with seats in the House and Senate. "We have no choice. We're stuck on the boat with him whether we like it or not," said a top Republican campaign official who's in contact with Trump's political operation. "Now, a rising tide raises all boats," the official added. "But the only ones who sound sure about the tide rising is the White House." Driving the news: At Trump's urging, the GOP on Wednesday and Thursday is hosting an unprecedented midterm convention in Dallas, headlined by the president. Zoom in : Trump plans to speak both nights at the convention. He's also the star of his political operation's first two TV ads: The first 30-second ad, called "Toughest Guy," is all about you-know-who. The second, labeled "Tax Cut Prices," features Trump as well and would be more conventional for a campaign in which he's on the ballot. Inside the room: Trump essentially demanded the ads focus on him because midterms are referendums on a president anyway, and he wanted to tout his accomplishments, The Atlantic first reported. "I'm not on the ballot but I'm on the ballot," Trump told one confidant who relayed the conversation to Axios. "Our job is to turn Trump voters into midterm voters," a Trump adviser told Axios. The intrigue: The ads look like a de facto compromise between Trump and his political staff. "This is for the audience of one," Trump's confidant said, referring to the president. "If the boss wants it, he gets it." One Trump adviser said to expect more conventional ads: "We will be stripping the bark off of Democrats and supporting our candidates. ... It's not all Trump-focused ads." What he's saying : On Friday, Trump acknowledged to reporters that "history has said that the sitting president" sees midterm losses, but he didn't complete the thought and then talked about how "nobody's ever had a first one and a half years like we have." "We have around $1 billion that I can spend," Trump said, referring to his super PAC and political nonprofit, which together have about $800 million. "I'm allocating, probably, about $400-$500 million" for the midterms, he said. "This is my money that I control now," he said. "I can spend it for what I want to spend it for. But I'm going to help a lot of the congressmen and senators that need help." Yes, but: It's unclear how Trump could spend that much money in two months. Between the lines: Trump's message in his tax cut ads is good, Republican strategists say, but their research increasingly shows voters blame him for the war in Iran that's raising gas prices. "Diesel's at an all-time high . Gas is about $4 a gallon. We can't message that away," said another Republican who runs campaigns for a few federal candidates. Trump advisers say he'll use the bully pulpit to make his case at the convention, but his speeches tend to lack cogency and focus, and their effectiveness is questionable. "If you look at the 20 competitive House races and the six Senate races we're really focused on, this is not as dire as the media wants you to think," a Trump adviser said. "This is winnable." The backstory: Trump explained this week on the "Lt. Dan" podcast with Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick that he decided to hold the event in Dallas because "we have this big convention for the presidential election, but the midterms — people talk about it. It's very important, but there's no convention." "So ... I just came up with the idea, and we raised a lot of money." Friction point : Trump's plummeting poll numbers aside, one problem is the convention's timing: It's competing with the NFL's season-opening games, which could draw far more attention. Even Republicans' interest is limited. Many candidates aren't going . "What's the point?" yet another Republican consultant involved in federal races told Axios. "It's like what they say about a tree falling in a forest: Does it make a noise if nobody's around? Well, is it a convention if no one's really watching?" What's next: At a Rose Garden dinner Wednesday with dozens of House Republicans, Trump promised to campaign across the country in 35 races "to see if we can get everyone elected." If Trump wants to campaign for a candidate, it's going to be hard for them to say no, said one of the consultants involved in talks with MAGA Inc., the super PAC that backs Trump. "Say no to Trump, and he could punish you," the consultant said. "Say yes to him, and his presence might not help. This is the world we're in."

entry.title: Fighter jet crashes at air show, killing 2 pilots with thousands of spectators watching - Fox News
entry.body: A day at the air show turned fatal on Saturday when a Greek air force jet crashed north of Athens as thousands of spectators watched. Both pilots were killed in the crash at Tanagra air force base but no civilians were hurt. The twin-seat Phantom F4 jet flew into the ground during a low-altitude maneuver just meters above the ground. EIGHT BELIEVED DEAD AFTER B-52 CRASHES SHORTLY AFTER TAKEOFF FROM EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE "The sense of grief is widespread, and our thoughts are with the families of the two pilots we lost," Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said. "It is a reminder of the daily danger faced by Greece’s aviators, who remain on constant standby to protect Greece's skies." The jet burst into flames on impact, sending up a large plume of black smoke, prompting 11 water-dropping planes and helicopters to assist 85 firefighters in extinguishing the blaze. 11 SKYDIVERS, ONE PILOT KILLED IN MISSOURI PLANE CRASH NEAR AIRPORT Video of the crash showed a second ball of fire nearby as the plane broke apart. The bodies of the pilots were eventually recovered. It hadn't been airborne for more than three minutes," an eyewitness told ERT, Greece’s state-owned broadcaster. The crash happened during the country’s annual Athens Flying Week. The organizers canceled the rest of the events following the incident and the area was evacuated. "It is with deep sadness that I learned of the death of the two officers of the Hellenic Air Force, who lost their lives in the tragic accident that occurred during the air show at Tanagra Air Base," Cyprus' Defense Minister Vasilis Palmas said, adding that he had called Nikos Dendias, Greece’s Minister of National Defense. AIR FORCE IDENTIFIES 8 CREW MEMBERS KILLED IN B-52 STRATOFORTRESS CRASH AT EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE The air force has declared three days of mourning in the country. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In May, two jets collided during an air show in Idaho, but the pilots were able to safely eject. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.
entry.summary: Fighter jet crashes at air show, killing 2 pilots with thousands of spectators watching Fox News Greek air force jet crashes at annual aerial show, starts fire ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Greek F-4 crashes during air show near Athens, two pilots dead, sources say Reuters Two pilots killed in Phantom F-4 jet crash during Greek air force annual show Euronews.com Fighter jet crashes in fireball at Greek airshow The Telegraph

entry.title: Fuel tanker blast in western Iran kills at least 10 - Al Jazeera
entry.body: Fuel tanker blast in western Iran kills at least 10 At least six other people were injured in the tanker blast on Iran’s Hamedan-Sanandaj highway, officials say. At least 10 people were killed in a fuel tanker blast in western Iran, Iranian national broadcast media (IRIB) reported. The tanker explosion on Saturday was triggered by a road crash on the Hamedan-Sanandaj highway. Recommended Stories list of 3 items - list 1 of 3US-Iran ceasefire? Not for Indian sailors being killed in Hormuz - list 2 of 3Diesel price hits all-time high in US amid Iran war woes - list 3 of 3Trump calls Iran war ‘small potatoes’, compares US deaths with Vietnam war The accident was caused by a technical fault in the braking system of the vehicle carrying the tanker, said the governor of Sanandaj, the capital of Iran’s Kurdistan province, as reported by the Reuters news agency. At least six other people were injured in the incident, the governor also said, adding that casualty figures were based on initial reports. According to local officials, the resulting fire was immediately brought under control. They did not provide further details on the identities of those killed. The latest deadly accident adds to a long history of deadly tanker and bus collisions in Iran, where poor road conditions, ageing vehicle fleets and heavy freight traffic have made such accidents a recurring hazard. At least 13 people were killed in 2018, after a fuel tanker slammed into a bus that had stopped to pick up passengers near Sanandaj. UNICEF said Iran’s rate of traffic crashes is 20 times the world’s average, as the country suffers from poor roads and lax traffic enforcement. According to a May 2017 report by the Tehran-based newspaper Financial Tribune, more than 20,000 people are killed and 800,000 are injured annually in road accidents in Iran.
entry.summary: Fuel tanker blast in western Iran kills at least 10 Al Jazeera Fuel tanker explosion after traffic accident kills 10 in Western Iran, state media says Reuters 11 killed, 7 injured in fuel tanker blast in western Iran Iran International Fuel tanker fire kills at least 11 in western Iran Middle East Eye 11 killed in fuel tanker explosion in Iran: State media The Tribune

entry.title: TV presenter among 11 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case - BBC
entry.body: TV presenter among 11 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case Egyptian television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people have been sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drugs charges. According to state-owned al-Ahram newspaper, they were part of a criminal gang which imported ingredients used to make drugs with the intent of selling them. They also had illegal firearms and munitions. Khalifa, 39, is best known for her TV programme Mission Impossible which dealt with crime issues. She has denied the charges. The verdict - which can be appealed against - was first announced last month. However, it was only confirmed a month later after the court obtained a religious opinion from the grand mufti of Egypt - a legal requirement in death sentence cases. During the trial, the court heard that authorities had seized more than 750kg (1,653lbs) of narcotics and the imported raw materials to make them. Twenty witnesses had given statements to the prosecutors, al-Ahram said, in addition to electronic evidence that included conversations and video clips. According to the state-run Akhbar al-Youm newspaper, when asked by the judge about her alleged role during a court appearance last September, Khalifa said she had never seen any drugs until she was photographed with them inside the anti-narcotics authority offices. According to a 2025 Amnesty International report, there were 492 death sentences in the course of the year, 23 of whom were executed. The defendants were found guilty of drug trafficking and rape, "crimes that did not amount to 'intentional killing' to which the use of the death penalty must be restricted under international law and standards", the report said.
entry.summary: TV presenter among 11 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case BBC Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime The Guardian Egypt sentences TV host to death by hanging over drug trafficking Ynetnews Mission Impossible presenter sentenced to death in drugs case abc.net.au Egyptian TV Presenter Sentenced to Death in Massive Drug Case Yahoo

entry.title: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway - BBC
entry.body: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway The Prince of Wales will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, Buckingham Palace has announced. Also going to the funeral, in a personal capacity, is Princess Anne, who is godmother to Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII. The late King Harald, a popular, modernising figure who had been on the Norwegian throne for 35 years, died last month at the age of 89. Royal sources say Prince William's attendance, representing his father King Charles, follows the convention that the monarch does not usually go to the funeral of another head of state. Large crowds are expected for the farewell to King Harald on 9 September, with a funeral procession to be followed by a service at Oslo Cathedral. Thousands have queued to pay their respects to the late king, during his lying in state in the chapel of the Royal Palace in the Norwegian capital. At the funeral, alongside Prince William, will be the widowed Queen Sonja, members of the Norwegian royal family including new King Haakon VIII, and other European royals. The service will be followed by a private burial in Norway's royal mausoleum in the Akershus Fortress. Among the tributes to King Harald was an emotional televised speech by his son King Haakon, who said: "Thank you for being such a good dad." Harald had been seen as a down to earth "people's king" who had helped to modernise the monarchy, broken with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure. His son said he represented the values of a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value". King Charles's message praised his cousin King Harald for serving his people with "unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility". King Haakon assumes his role at a difficult time, with the Norwegian royal family facing scandals this year. His wife, Queen Mette-Marit, came under scrutiny when it was revealed she had maintained a three-year friendship with the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised. Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. While Prince William will be in Norway, King Charles has returned to Scotland, after meeting President Macron of France at the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London this week. The King will be hosting Andy Burnham at Balmoral this weekend, in the traditional annual visit of the prime minister to stay with the monarch.
entry.summary: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway BBC Prince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway’s King Harald V The Guardian Princess Astrid of Norway alone with her brother's coffin: The last of her generation says goodbye to King Harald HOLA Prince William and Princess Royal to attend King Harald’s funeral The Telegraph Why King Charles will not attend the funeral of Norway’s King Harald The Independent

entry.title: Judge reinforces order halting immediate work on Trump’s 250-foot arch - usatoday.com
entry.body: Judge reinforces order halting immediate work on Trump’s 250-foot arch A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Friday, Sept. 4, to provide 48 hours’ notice before moving forward with work on the site of a planned 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that the administration must inform the court “before engaging in any activity on Memorial Circle other than on-site information gathering” to identify underground cultural artifacts. Chutkan reinforced her order a day after Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum announced plans on Sept. 3 to break ground at the site of the arch in the coming days. “We are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck, at Memorial Circle on Columbia Island between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery,” Burgum wrote on X. “This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World.” The proposed arch, one of several projects Trump has launched in an effort to change the landscape of the nation’s capital, has been controversial from the start. A group of three veterans and a historian filed a lawsuit in February to oppose the project. The plaintiffs asked Chutkan on Sept. 4 to issue a 14-day restraining order to block the Trump administration from “taking any steps to construct or to direct or facilitate construction of any structure in Memorial Circle.” Despite Burgum’s announcement, the government argued in a court filing that the planned activity at the site of the proposed arch is standard archaeological survey work. The administration intends to mechanically excavate four test pits no earlier than Sept. 21 and the land is expected to be restored by Oct. “This activity is not construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, of an arch,” the government said. The proposed arch is also awaiting final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, which would need to grant an exception to a 130-foot building height limit.
entry.summary: Judge reinforces order halting immediate work on Trump’s 250-foot arch usatoday.com Is Work Starting for Trump’s Arch? It Depends Who’s Asking. entry.title: The next James Bond: the (00)7 questions fans want answered
entry.body: The next James Bond: the (00)7 questions fans want answered - Published James Bond is special. Playing him propels an actor into an exceptionally elite group of performers. From Sean Connery to Daniel Craig, only six people have ever played him in the official film series. In the last decade alone the UK has had more prime ministers, and twice as many people have walked on the moon than have played the British secret agent. The last announcement of a new Bond was 21 years ago in 2005. So it's inevitable for Bond fans to want to have their questions answered about the future of one of cinema's most sought after roles, in one of cinema's biggest franchises. Who will be the next person to play 007? 1 of 11 This is, of course, the big question fans have been talking about for the last six years. And with an announcement edging closer and closer, the speculation has intensified recently. Many of the same well-known faces have been bandied about for months, if not years. Those names have generally included Henry Cavill, Harris Dickinson, Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden, James Norton, Jack O'Connell, Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson. More recently, other names have also been thrown into the mix. Earlier this year Variety reported that stage actor Tom Francis had auditioned, external for the role. And in late August Page Six claimed there will be more auditions this month, and that Gladiator 2 star Paul Mescal and Heartstopper and SAS: Rogue Heroes star Jack Barton are also on the audition list, external. The announcement about the next film's producers referred to keeping Bond's spirit alive "as he embarks on his next adventure", seemingly confirming that Bond would remain male. However, it's never been clear whether the rumoured names have been well-sourced inside information, or merely guesswork and speculation. Have the auditions started yet? Back in May, Amazon MGM Studios who now control the Bond franchise confirmed the casting process was under way, external. But little detail beyond that was given, the statement only saying: "While we don't plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we're excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right." It now seems that the right time is fast approaching. In an interview with Deadline, external Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, was asked whether we might have news on who would be playing Bond by the end of the year. She replied: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet." Last month entertainment writer Daniel Richtman said, external on social media: "I hear they're in the final round of casting for James Bond and might have already found their guy." His post on X was followed up by journalist Jeff Sneider, external who said: "Heard the same rumour. First it was down to seven, then three. Now 'they may have found their guy'. Who knows at this point? But for some reason, I don't think it's any of the so-called frontrunners, including the Aussieâ¦" The Aussie is almost certainly a reference to Euphoria and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi, who was brought up in Brisbane and Melbourne before moving to the US to pursue his acting career. How do the auditions work? The audition process is likely to have been carried out in a similar way to previous castings. The scene that many would-be Bonds have traditionally had to peform is taken from From Russia With Love, where 007 comes out of his bathroom to find Tatiana Romanova in his bed. It's a scene where an actor relies on their physical presence, movement and charisma. No explosions fights or gadgets. As GoldenEye and Casino Royale director Martin Campbell explained to entertainment website Gold Derby, external: "The word is effortless. You never see Bond fumble, he is very economic, efficient and effortless. That scene covers all the bases, basically." And for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen. As the 007 team themselves have explained in the past, external: "Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors." 4. How will the new Bond be announced? Generally, the unveiling of a new Bond has taken place at a London press conference in front of the world's media. But for the first time creative control of the franchise is in the hands of a studio like Amazon MGM. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond. And they're reported to have paid at least $20m more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future. Having paid such eye-watering amounts, it seems more than possible that Amazon MGM might well wish to drive fans towards their streaming service, with any reveal of the new Bond being exclusively announced on Prime Video. It would almost certainly see a surge in streaming subscriptions. And such an announcement would still inevitably be covered by the world's press. Global James Bond Day on 5 October, the 64th anniversary of the release of the first film Dr No, is fast approaching. So this date might be a good day for fans to mark in their diaries for a possible announcement. What is known about the next film? We don't yet know what it will be called, or have a confirmed release date. Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight is currently writing the script, and Dune's Denis Villeneuve will direct. They and the team may well already have a title in mind. Or, of course, they may just be calling it Bond 26 for now. Most of the series have taken titles from the original Ian Fleming stories. Four of those remain unused - The Hildebrand Rarity, Risico, 007 in New York, and The Property of a Lady. Although elements from those stories have already been used in previous Bond films. Fans have also been busy putting forward their own suggestions for potential titles. Since the accession of King Charles III in 2022, those suggestions have included On His Majesty's Secret Service, and King & Country. As for a release date, it's been widely reported that the next film is likely to be released in 2028. That means it's almost certain that this will be the biggest ever gap between films, more than the six years and four months between 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye. How far ahead are the Bond team planning? Only the Bond team themselves really know this. But Amazon MGM do have the financial resources to plan well ahead, and explore various issues, such as how Bond will operate over multiple films; will there be an overriding arc that will cover his journey over the next decade etc; will there be a film every two years, every three years, every four or five? Additionally, with such a huge investment, AmazonMGM will undoubtedly be keen to learn from Disney's experiences with Star Wars, and Marvel's experiences with its Marvel Cinematic Universe, in how best to use the Bond franchise. While there might be appetite for multiple Bond spin-offs, eg Young Bond, the Miss Moneypenny adventures etc, they will also be wary that they don't over-saturate the market, and damage the films which are at the core of the Bond franchise. How will the next film deal with the ending of the last? The below contains spoilers for No Time To Die Daniel Craig's farewell at the end of No Time To Die saw him on the island lair of the film's villain, Rami Malek's Safin, as it was struck by a volley of air strikes, with the super spy apparently finally meeting his demise. Rumours have indicated that the next film might well reflect Bond's early years at the start of his MI6 career, in effect a reboot, which means that there won't be any pressure or sense of disappointment that the story won't reflect No Time To Die's conclusion. And in any case, Bond fans have been reassured by the message that has appeared at the end of almost every Bond film - "James Bond will return". It looks like soon we'll be finding out who that James Bond will be.
entry.summary: Speculation has been building recently that an announcement about Daniel Craig's successor could be close.

entry.title: Aviation faces hotter, stormier skies – and passengers might have to accept more disruption
entry.body: He warns of a situation where traffic is diverted from Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Stansted at the same time, leaving aircraft coming in across the Atlantic and a large number of European flights all looking for somewhere to land at the same time, and some with dwindling fuel reserves. This would at the very least create serious disruption for passengers, who might end up hundreds of miles from their destinations. But it could also, he thinks, create "a very serious risk event, such as an aircraft running out of fuel in the sky". Aircraft are legally required to carry enough fuel to take them to an alternative airport if necessary, and to allow them to fly for an extra 30 minutes on top of that. Not everyone shares Atkinson's concern. Former airline executive Andrew Charlton, who manages the Swiss-based consultancy Aviation Advocacy, thinks the risk is low.
entry.summary: Are people going to have to increasingly accept more delays and diversions as the effects of climate change intensify?

entry.title: Are Stocks Going to Plunge if Congress Is Split Under President Donald Trump? Here's What History Says About Stock Market Returns in This Scenario. - Yahoo Finance
entry.body: In comparison, the 34 years that featured a Republican president and a divided government (meaning one or both houses of Congress controlled by Democrats) yielded an average annual return of just 7.33% for the S&P 500. While there's no indication that stocks will plunge if Election Night produces a split Congress, nearly a century of history shows that more modest stock returns should be expected in its wake. Stocks thrive, regardless of the party in power At any given time, several catalysts threaten to upend the stock market, such as rapidly rising outstanding margin debt and premium valuations. From time to time, these headwinds can lead to stock market corrections and even a short-lived plunge. The makeup of Congress is rarely, if ever, responsible for these elevator-down moves. While historical data shows that certain congressional makeups are more favorable than others, the average annual return of the Dow Jones Industrial Average or S&P 500 is decisively positive, no matter how the puzzle pieces are arranged.

entry.body: But President Trump has pushed American energy dominance, we are producing more energy now than in the past." Duffy added that "it's only President Trump who's trying to drive these prices down," even though the president's war has been the primary reason they've been going up. Fox & Friends weekend host Charlie Hurt gives Trump credit for record high diesel prices: "Uhhh, they'd be a lot higher if it wasn't for the efforts of the administration" "When you look at diesel, you have to look at Russia and Ukraine," Duffy replies 🥴 pic.twitter.com/Wm5bLJ6exA — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) September 5, 2026 As a report published Friday by The Associated Press explained, the cost of diesel has a particularly strong impact on the price of food since the fuel is used to power both farm equipment and the trucks used to deliver food to grocery stores.
