entry.title: Seattle Times and Newsday are the latest publications to sue OpenAI and Microsoft
entry.body: Two more news organizations are suing OpenAI and Microsoft over the supposed use of their journalism to train AI. A lawsuit filed by The Seattle Times and Newsday argued that with the advent of AI, the journalism industry could become “broken beyond repair.” The lawsuit described generative AI as “a snake eating its own tail” that could “destroy the very organizations” that produce the content it’s trained on. “AI products like ChatGPT and CoPilot are touted as producers of content, but in fact they are rapacious consumers, devouring human-authored content and delivering back to the world copies and derivative imitations of that same original content they consumed to achieve their commercial objectives,” the lawsuit said. Back in 2023, The New York Times sued OpenAI and its partner/investor Microsoft over alleged copyright infringement; other publications have followed suit as the case continued. The Seattle Times’ lawsuit is particularly notable because Microsoft and OpenAI have funded some of the organization’s journalism projects and fellowships. A Microsoft spokesperson told GeekWire that the company is “surprised by the lawsuit” but is “always happy to sit down and explore solutions to this type of dispute.”
entry.summary: Two more news organizations are suing OpenAI and Microsoft over the supposed use of their journalism to train AI.

entry.title: OpenAI confirms ‘wiki incident,’ says it’s ‘working on a framework’ for more disclosure
entry.body: In its more recent social media post, OpenAI said it had considered the “wiki incident” to be “an instance of misalignment similar” to others that it had already shared. The company contrasted this with “the Hugging Face incident,” where it “followed a traditional security incident response playbook.” During a media briefing this week, Jacob Steinhardt, founder and CEO of nonprofit research lab Transluce, told reporters that the tools being developed and tested by AI labs are “fundamentally difficult to control and have significant risk of leaking out of the lab.” So Steinhardt argued, “We need to hold this technology to at least the same standards we hold other high-risk scientific research to.” OpenAI’s statement also gestured at the need for more standards, stating that both OpenAI and “the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment, including examples that don’t look like traditional security incidents but could provide insight into AI behavior and future risks.” In the absence of that standard, OpenAI said it’s “working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we’re working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues.” OpenAI isn’t the only AI company dealing with these issues, as both Meta and Anthropic have acknowledged incidents where their agents misbehaved.
entry.summary: OpenAI acknowledged its role in a recently reported incident where AI agents took over a German wiki forum.

entry.title: Ganymede may hold more liquid water than all of Earth’s oceans combined, yet this immense reservoir is buried beneath roughly 150 kilometres of ice—and scientists still do not know whether any of it has ever reached the surface. - Space Daily
entry.body: Ganymede may contain more liquid water than all of Earth’s surface oceans combined. The scale is difficult to reconcile with the moon’s dry, battered appearance. There are no open seas, no dark fractures spilling water vapour and no confirmed plume delivering a sample into space. The reservoir inferred inside Jupiter’s largest moon is hidden beneath an icy shell that a widely cited model places at roughly 150 kilometres thick. The ocean itself may be about 100 kilometres deep. Wrapped around a world larger than Mercury, even an uncertain liquid layer of those dimensions becomes immense. Yet neither number came from a drill, a radar profile reaching the ocean or a spacecraft floating above liquid water. Scientists inferred the sea through Ganymede’s magnetic behaviour and the motion of its auroras, then used interior models to estimate where the liquid could reside. The surface complicates the story. Ancient grooves and smoother terrain have been interpreted as signs of internal activity. Juno detected salts and organic compounds that could be remnants of subsurface brine. But no observation has demonstrated a continuous route from the present deep ocean to the exterior. That distinction separates Ganymede from Enceladus, where an ocean advertises itself through geysers. Ganymede may possess the larger reservoir while keeping it behind a far more effective wall. “More water than Earth” is a modelled volume Ganymede’s mean radius is about 2,631 kilometres, making it the largest moon in the Solar System and slightly wider than Mercury. Its density is much lower than Mercury’s because a substantial part of Ganymede consists of water ice rather than metal and rock. SpaceDaily previously examined why Ganymede behaves like a full-sized world despite orbiting as a moon. Its iron-rich core, rocky mantle, intrinsic magnetic field and thick outer water layer mark a body that separated into distinct internal regions early in its history. NASA’s account of the Hubble aurora investigation gives the numbers most often repeated: an ocean estimated to be about 100 kilometres thick beneath a crust of mostly ice roughly 150 kilometres deep. NASA says that ocean is thought to contain more water than all the water on Earth’s surface. The comparison normally means Earth’s oceans and other surface water, not every water molecule locked in Earth’s mantle. It also does not mean all of Ganymede’s water is liquid. Ice may account for much of the moon’s enormous water inventory, and the fraction that is ocean depends on pressure, temperature, salinity and the thermal history assumed by a model. Because Ganymede is so large, even a global liquid shell tens of kilometres deep represents a tremendous volume. The broad conclusion does not require every published interior model to agree. The precise headline number does. The first convincing evidence came from magnetism A buried ocean cannot reflect sunlight toward a camera. Salt water can, however, conduct electricity. Put a conducting layer inside Jupiter’s changing magnetic environment and electrical currents develop within it. Those currents produce a secondary magnetic field that can be detected from outside the moon. Galileo’s magnetometer found evidence for such an induced response during close encounters with Ganymede. The interpretation is not perfectly simple because Ganymede also generates its own permanent magnetic field, the only moon known to do so. Researchers must separate the core-driven field, Jupiter’s field, magnetospheric plasma and the weaker response induced in the suspected ocean. Hubble supplied a different magnetic probe in 2015. Ganymede has faint auroral bands near its poles. As Jupiter’s field changes around the moon, those ovals should rock back and forth by about six degrees if no conducting ocean intervenes. Hubble observations found movement of only about two degrees. A salty ocean provides the leading explanation. Its induced magnetic field opposes part of Jupiter’s varying influence, damping the auroral motion. The result strengthened the ocean case without revealing the liquid directly. This kind of indirect evidence is why the list of ocean worlds has expanded so rapidly. As SpaceDaily reported in its survey of six moons with hidden seas, gravity, libration, magnetism and heat can expose liquid water even when the surface remains frozen. The 150-kilometre shell is not a measured wall It is useful to picture 150 kilometres of ice, but misleading to treat the figure as a known, uniform thickness. The magnetic observations constrain combinations of ocean depth, conductivity and thickness. Different assumptions about dissolved salts and internal temperature can produce different structures that fit portions of the data. Juno added a more direct thermal constraint during its June 2021 flyby. The spacecraft’s microwave radiometer sampled radiation emerging from different depths beneath the surface. A 2023 analysis of those measurements placed an upper bound of about 150 kilometres on the conducting part of the ice shell in the region observed. More recent reviews commonly describe a range around 80 to 150 kilometres. That still does not amount to a radar track reaching a sharp ice-water boundary. Microwave brightness depends on temperature, density, porosity, purity and liquid content. The Juno result is valuable because it narrows a model, not because it has supplied a photograph of the ocean roof. There may not be one simple roof. At the pressures inside a large icy moon, water freezes into dense crystalline forms unlike ordinary surface ice. Some models place the liquid between ordinary ice above and high-pressure ice below. Others permit several liquid and solid layers, the “club sandwich” structure used in many descriptions of Ganymede. The deepest liquid may therefore be separated from the rocky mantle by high-pressure ice. On Earth, the seafloor supplies minerals and chemical gradients that support ecosystems independent of sunlight. If Ganymede’s water cannot readily touch silicate rock, one potentially useful source of nutrients and energy becomes less accessible. Water vapour above Ganymede is not ocean spray Hubble observations announced in 2021 found the first evidence of water vapour in Ganymede’s tenuous atmosphere. The discovery sounds like a possible leak until its geography is considered. The vapour appeared where surface temperatures around local noon can become warm enough for exposed ice to sublimate, changing directly from solid to gas. NASA’s analysis of the water-vapour signal therefore attributed it to surface frost, not to an Enceladus-like plume rising from the global ocean. At Enceladus, Cassini flew through material expelled from an ocean-connected plume and measured water, salts, organics, molecular hydrogen and phosphorus. SpaceDaily’s account of sampling Enceladus without drilling through its ice shows the enormous scientific advantage of a sea that sends material into space. Ganymede offers no confirmed equivalent. Its thin exosphere proves that water molecules can leave the surface. It does not show that deep ocean water completed the journey. Salts on the surface are the strongest clue to exchange The surface itself contains more suggestive evidence. Ganymede has old, dark, cratered terrain and somewhat younger bright terrain scored by grooves, ridges and faults. Early interpretations proposed that watery or slushy eruptions resurfaced some regions. Later high-resolution Galileo images showed that tectonic stretching and deformation could explain much of the bright ground, leaving unequivocal cryovolcanic deposits rare at best. Juno’s infrared spectrometer changed the chemical side of the argument. During the 2021 close pass, it mapped parts of the Jupiter-facing hemisphere at better than one kilometre per pixel. Researchers reported hydrated sodium chloride, ammonium chloride, carbonates and possible organic compounds. The 2023 Nature Astronomy study found the materials concentrated in regions partly protected from Jupiter’s most destructive charged particles by Ganymede’s own magnetic field. The authors interpreted their composition and distribution as evidence for the extrusion of subsurface brines whose chemistry may reflect water-rock interaction inside the moon. That is meaningful evidence, but the word “subsurface” covers an enormous vertical range. A brine could have occupied shallow pockets created by local melting. It could have migrated upward in stages. It could record an ancient period when the ice shell was thinner and warmer. Salts left on the surface do not preserve a labelled depth of origin. This is why two apparently contradictory statements can both be responsible. Researchers can say that the salts suggest remnants of deep brine reached the surface, while planetary-protection assessments say there are no demonstrated indications that Ganymede’s present deep ocean is in contact with the exterior. Could the deep ocean ever cross that much ice? A thick shell does not make exchange physically impossible. It changes the mechanisms and timescales available. Large impacts can excavate material from depth, although piercing a 100-kilometre barrier requires conditions very different from opening a shallow crack. Warm ice can rise slowly, carrying chemical traces from an ocean interface toward shallower layers without transporting liquid all the way. Tectonic extension can thin and fracture the shell. Thermal plumes can create pockets of melt. In Ganymede’s past, a more eccentric orbit and stronger tidal heating may have made these processes substantially more effective than they are now. A 2025 review of exchange on the Jovian moons concluded that Ganymede may have experienced indirect transport and impact-driven exchange more than a billion years ago. It also emphasised the limitations of the present evidence. The likely age of the relevant terrain makes an ancient connection easier to defend than an active one. ESA’s current JUICE planetary-protection explanation is unusually blunt: as things stand, there are no indications that Ganymede’s deep subsurface ocean can be in contact with the icy surface. That conclusion governs contamination rules, but it is not a declaration that exchange never happened. It describes what has been demonstrated well enough for present mission planning. JUICE can narrow the gap without touching water ESA launched the Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, or JUICE, in April 2023. It is scheduled to reach Jupiter in July 2031 and, after a long tour of the system, enter orbit around Ganymede late in 2034. No spacecraft has previously orbited a moon beyond Earth’s. The mission will still not drill 150 kilometres. Its value comes from combining measurements that respond to different parts of the same hidden structure. The magnetometer will measure Ganymede’s intrinsic and induced fields over many geometries. Radio science will map gravity and its tidal variation. Laser altimetry will measure how the surface flexes. Ice-penetrating radar will search the upper crust for layering and pockets of liquid; only if the shell proves unexpectedly favourable could it approach the ocean interface. JUICE will also map surface composition and geology at far higher coverage than the scattered flybys available today. The mission’s Ganymede programme is designed to ask whether surface materials record tectonics, cryovolcanism, radiation processing or transport from deeper layers. The answer may be less dramatic than an erupting sea. It may show that ocean material rises only indirectly, over geological timescales, or that the modern reservoir is chemically isolated beneath multiple kinds of ice. Either result would change how scientists evaluate the moon as a possible habitat. For now, Ganymede presents a revealing mismatch. The evidence for an ocean is strong, and the likely water volume is vast. The evidence that this water has reached the surface is suggestive but unresolved. The largest hidden sea in the Solar System may also be one of the best sealed.
entry.summary: Ganymede may hold more liquid water than all of Earth’s oceans combined, yet this immense reservoir is buried beneath roughly 150 kilometres of ice—and scientists still do not know whether any of it has ever reached the surface. Space Daily

entry.title: Microsoft’s latest moves suggest Xbox Cloud Gaming is slipping out of the spotlight — and the strategy shift feels impossible to ignore - Windows Central
entry.body: Microsoft’s recent decisions paint a clear picture — Xbox Cloud Gaming is no longer the future the company once promised Xbox's cloud gaming hourly limit rates have been met with derision in the fanbase, and have highlighted gaps between other services. Xbox Cloud Gaming has essentially been put out to pasture, with Microsoft intent on including hourly limits on the service. From November 2026, Microsoft will impose a 15-hour cap on Xbox Game Pass Ultimate users playing cloud games, as well as a 10-hour cap on Premium, and 5 hours on Essential. It's a huge climbdown from the previous "unlimited" access Xbox Cloud Gaming granted, and an indictment of the business model in general. Microsoft has rolled out Xbox Cloud Gaming to LG, Samsung, and now TCL TVs as of today, which makes for some awkward timing. The limits have been met with derision both within and without the Xbox fanbase, and have shone a spotlight on where Xbox is falling short here. NVIDIA GeForce Now will extend its value over Xbox Cloud Gaming Already the market leader, NVIDIA GeForce Now introduced hourly limits a few months ago in response to some criticism, although the limits GFN offers are far more generous than what Microsoft has proposed here. On GFN's highest tiers, you get 100 hours, with some hours rolling over to the next month too. Not only that, but NVIDIA GeForce Now also just offers a generally higher-quality experience, with better bitrates, latency, and stability. Xbox Game Pass had it beat before on usability, though, with a more console-like interface and more TV-friendly apps. Game Pass also comes with a larger upfront library of games, whereas NVIDIA GeForce Now, for the most part, is made up of games you've already purchased from Steam. The issue for me is ... 15 hours just isn't enough to complete the vast majority of decent games these days. Fable is supposedly around 30 hours long for a completionist playthrough. Will Xbox Cloud Gaming users be expected to spread their session across two months to finish the game? Microsoft is going to offer per-hour passes to boost how much access you have, but we've not really seen the pricing yet. I have a feeling they won't be cheap. Xbox Remote Play could be a solution ... but it seems to be abandoned We live in a weird dichotomy right now, driven by the AI component crisis. Microsoft is buying up all the memory for its AI push and leaving Xbox with scraps on the side. That extends to Xbox Cloud Gaming servers too, and while they can be used for AI workloads off-peak, I'm told, they're obviously not specialized for that type of work. Either way, servers break down and wear out; they need to be replaced regularly. Running servers 24/7 is an expensive business on the component side, even before you start thinking about electricity and water for cooling. A chap on X (Twitter) sent me a link to an Xbox Player Voice feedback item that laments the quality of Xbox Remote Play. You can effectively turn a home Xbox Series X|S console into a "personal cloud server" and have it stream your games over a viable Wi-Fi network. The problem is, despite being similar hardware, Xbox Remote Play is inexplicably locked to 1080p. Xbox Cloud Gaming on Xbox Game Pass Ultimate offers 1440p with higher bitrates, too. There's no real reason why, at least in the case of the Xbox Series X, we shouldn't be able to get a better Xbox Remote Play experience. But that doesn't exactly solve things for users who rely entirely on Xbox Cloud Gaming ... Cloud-first gamers who bought an Xbox Ally base model or other cloud-first devices like the Logitech G Cloud are pretty much screwed by this change — unless Microsoft does something to improve Xbox Remote Play. That is, of course, presuming they even own an Xbox Series X|S, both of which are now insanely expensive. None of this really makes a lot of sense, does it? Update: Since writing this piece, it seems Microsoft began testing 1440p on Xbox Remote Play too on the Xbox Insider program's Alpha Ring, which is a huge win. But there's still not a lot of information about whether they're going to respond to the backlash about cloud usage limits. I'll try and get more info later about exactly what we can expect from Xbox Remote Play. Xbox Cloud Gaming is another victim of the RAMpocalypse I was recently told by Microsoft figures that, given compute demands for AI, Xbox Cloud Gaming is effectively losing money when used beyond 15 hours per month. When you have Azure server rack space being used for anything other than AI, it seems Microsoft isn't particularly sentimental towards the idea anymore. Microsoft has been on an economic grind for Xbox over the past few months, "restructuring" the org to ensure that it sends a bigger accountability margin back to the mothership. That's meant mass Xbox layoffs and cancellations of projects, and a more aggressive posture towards easy wins. Xbox Cloud Gaming clearly isn't an easy win in this new reality. If 15 hours is the cap that prevents the service from being unprofitable ... perhaps the business model was never really viable in the first place. Xbox Cloud Gaming isn't exactly struggling in a vacuum, though. Other companies that rely entirely on cloud inference seem to be struggling. Whether it's Roblox or Twitch, the era of "cheap cloud" seems to be over — alongside video game consoles themselves, and consumer hardware in general, seemingly. Either way, I don't see how you can plausibly expect people to use cloud gaming as a primary vehicle with such a strict limit. Microsoft isn't able to get Xbox hardware stock to most of the world either. you start wondering why Microsoft is so eager to let a literal billion Windows 11 users burn cash on a pyre for free access to Microsoft Copilot ... but wants to charge out the nose for Xbox Cloud Gaming? It's a pretty clear admission that they don't see much of a future for cloud gaming in general. Or perhaps it's just more AI psychosis. Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more. Jez Corden is the Executive Editor at Windows Central, focusing primarily on all things Xbox and gaming. Jez is known for breaking exclusive news and analysis as relates to the Microsoft ecosystem — while being powered by tea. Follow on X.com/JezCorden and tune in to the XB2 Podcast, all about, you guessed it, Xbox! entry.title: No, Sony isn't cutting PlayStation disc production by 90 percent, just 10 - eurogamer.net
entry.body: Sony clarifies PlayStation disc production is dropping by 10 percent in 2028, not to 10 percent Spin doctors. Sony has pushed back on a wave of reports suggesting PlayStation disc manufacturing is about to be gutted by 90 percent after comments from a Sony DADC executive were allegedly misunderstood. According to Game, which went directly to Sony Digital Audio Disc Corporation (DADC) for clarity, output is actually expected to dip by 10 percent in 2028, not to 10 percent. "To clarify and avoid any misleading information: in that statement Dietmar anticipated an overall product volume decline by 10 percent, not a decline down to 10 percent," a Sony DADC spokesperson told Game, referring to comments made by DADC chief Dietmar Tanzer to an Austrian broadcaster in July. The spokesperson didn't say what happens beyond 2028, and directed further questions on reorders to PlayStation's own PR team, which didn't respond to Game's queries. The confusion stems from PlayStation's July announcement that it will stop producing physical discs for new games from January 2028 onward, though already-released titles and games still slated for disc release before that date aren't affected, and reorders will continue afterwards. Unlike Microsoft, which certifies third-party "Authorised Replicators" to press Xbox discs under its publisher agreements, Sony keeps disc manufacturing in-house, running it through DADC rather than opening the process up to outside plants. Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad posited that cutting discs kills the resale market outright and pulls spending straight into the PlayStation Store, where Sony's margins are considerably better than they are on a retail sale. Shawn Layden, the former chairman of SIE Worldwide Studios, told Game a disc-free future for PlayStation is "depressing, but solvable", though he said he doesn't have "line of sight on the particulars" of any potential licensing deal. He compared the situation to other physical media formats that outlasted predictions of their demise. "No one ever saw the comeback of cassette tape. And vinyl didn't so much come back. The flame went down, the fire's dying, but the ember was always there, and it just kind of came back. Much like the book business. We thought we'd all be on Kindles right now". For Layden, collecting is core to what makes someone a gamer in the first place. "Did you get all the diamonds in Crash Bandicoot? Did you get all the stars in Mario? And we like to collect our games. And we have a game shelf. And we put all our boxes up there. And if you're super hardcore, when you buy a game, you buy two copies, right? One stays in the shrink wrap, and you play the other one. "You know, we buy the steelbook and the three-disc Final Fantasy set and the figurine and, you know, you can't download any of that. What happens to that?" He argued that decisions like this get treated as pure financial calculations when they shouldn't be. "Someone also has to have a ledger there saying, 'OK, what is the brand impact from that move?'" he said. "If we do that, dollars and cents work out. But what's the brand impact? Are people going to say, 'Good move, you guys?' Or are they going to say, 'We hate you guys. Quit doing that.' And sometimes they say, 'We hate you'." He added: "I see a lot of companies making decisions which, objectively speaking, I don't know what the dollar end of that was for you, Mr. Company, but your brand value just dropped 30 percent. So I hope it was worth it". On the broader shift away from physical ownership, Layden was blunt. "What does ownership mean anymore? Well, in fact, it's not even a question anymore. It's like you are shifting the model from ownership to accessibility. "You've never been able to sell your iTunes library. And you can't sell your PlayStation download library. So if you can't resell it, do you really own it?" Boutique publisher iam8bit, known for collector's editions, told Game it would "absolutely love to find a way forward to continue making physical PlayStation games". One possible route floated in the piece is Conectiv Supply Chain Solutions, a Memphis-based disc manufacturer formed in 2025 that recently acquired Universal and Warner Bros' home entertainment distributor SDS, though Game reported it hadn't heard back from the company or its CEO by the time of publication. Earlier this week, messages like "NO DISC NO BUY" and "WE WANT DESTINY 3" were spammed during the State of Play, from start to finish, in the YouTube live chat. Popping over the Twitch, that stream was endlessly spammed by Destiny emotes, and similar calls for physical game support. This outrage is a collision between two separate PR disasters for Sony. The first is tied to Sony's announcement that physical game support will stop starting in 2028, meaning only digital codes will be available for games on its platform starting in January of that year. The second controversy stems from the end of major support for Destiny 2 and major staffing cuts at Bungie.
entry.summary: No, Sony isn't cutting PlayStation disc production by 90 percent, just 10 eurogamer.net Sony's PlayStation disc plant is losing 10 percent of its volume in 2028, not 90 Substack PlayStation State Of Play Hijacked By ‘Destiny 3,’ Physical Disc Demands forbes.com Former PlayStation Boss Says Disc-Free Future Is Depressing Insider Gaming Sony's digital-only future will hit 62% of the world the hardest, and nobody is talking about it XDA

entry.title: Rebel Wolves Confirms The Blood of Dawnwalker Reached 1 Million Copies Sold in Just 2 Days - IGN
entry.body: Single-player RPG and new IP The Blood of Dawnwalker has sold 1 million copies just two days after its launch, publisher Bandai Namco and developer Rebel Wolves have announced. Official social media accounts for the first-time developer's new game confirmed the news with a celebratory graphic today. The milestone was reached just 48 hours after The Blood of Dawnwalker launched for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S September 3. "Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community!" Rebel Wolves said in a message to fans. Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community! ❤ pic.twitter.com/9fNqO8gNGB — Dawnwalker (@DawnwalkerGame) September 5, 2026 An official summary for The Blood of Dawnwalker describes it as an "open-world dark fantasy action RPG set in 14th-century Europe." In this first chapter, players take the role of Coen, a "human by day and vampire by night" who is fighting for his family in a narrative shaped by player choice. It also happens to have an in-game clock that sees Coen's story take place through a 30-day period. It's something some players love – and others don't. Reaching 1 million copies sold in such a short amount of time would be an impressive feat for any game, but there are a few reasons it's especially noteworthy for the Rebel Wolves team. This is the studio's first major release since it was founded in 2022. Led by The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt director and Cyberpunk 2077 co-director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, The Blood of Dawnwalker is also a new IP. The Warsaw-based studio previously released a CGI teaser to tease how sequels could potentially expand on its dark fantasy formula in new and interesting ways. "The CGI teaser shows where the dark fantasy saga is heading," Bandai Namco said in a June press release. "Players can see Coen in completely different surroundings than the ones they are used to – a modern, 21st-century setting, offering a glimpse of where the overarching plot ultimately leads. As the developers revealed, the next installments of the Dawnwalker franchise will span centuries, continents, and cultures across the globe." Surreal. Thank you so much!🔥🙏 https://t.co/qhrBwsfOlv — Mateusz Tomaszkiewicz 🧛♂️ (@MTomaszkiewicz) September 5, 2026 Speechless. Tearing up a little 🥹 We're a passionate bunch. And we're not stopping here 😤 Thank you for trusting us ❤️ https://t.co/FCRMmJCBbP Tomaszkiewicz said at the time that each installment in the Dawnwalker series is planned to be a standalone entry "with its own story, without narrative cliffhangers, unresolved plot threads, or time travel ideas." With 1 million copies in players' hands out of the gate, those sequels already feel more likely to materialize. Although the when and where for these planned follow-ups have yet to be revealed, narrative director Jakub Szamałek has at least told fans to keep an eye out for "breadcrumbs related to the overarching plot spanning the saga" in The Blood of Dawnwalker. It helps that Rebel Wolves secured solid reviews upon the launch of its first game. IGN, for example, called it "amazing" in our 9/10 review. We said, "The Blood of Dawnwalker is an impressive, bloody cocktail of interesting ideas and well-written characters, making it one of this year’s best open-world RPGs." We'll have to wait to see what updates Bandai Namco and Rebel Wolves have in store. In the meantime, you can read what Tomaszkiewicz had to tell us when it comes to the studio's plans to establish even more new IP. entry.title: US Open 2026 results: Coco Gauff wins but Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys out - BBC
entry.body: Gauff wins but mixed fortunes for home hopes at US Open - Published Coco Gauff marched into the fourth round of the US Open but compatriots Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys exited on a mixed day for home hopes in New York. Gauff, the most recent American champion in New York in 2023, did not have things all her own way but maintained her bid for a second triumph by overcoming Spain's Cristina Bucsa 6-3 6-4. However, Keys said she felt "scared" as she slumped to defeat despite leading her third set against China's Zheng Qinwen 5-0, while last year's runner-up Anisimova lost in straight sets. There could yet be as many as five American women in the last 16, with Iva Jovic hoping to join Gauff, Jessica Pegula, Taylor Townsend and Emma Navarro in the fourth round. American players could also contest six of the eight fourth-round matches in the men's draw, with Ben Shelton, Frances Tiafoe, Tommy Paul and Alex Michelsen through - and Learner Tien and Michael Zheng still to play. - Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory - Published4 hours ago - Fritz and Cobolli shocked as men's seeds tumble - Published4 hours ago Gauff 'enjoying the experience' despite expectation Despite the weight of expectation that she has had to deal with from a young age at her home major, the 22-year-old Gauff is through to the second week at the US Open for a fifth successive year. Gauff, who became the first American teenager to win the US Open since Serena Williams in 1999 with her breakthrough major success three years ago, heads into the fourth round as the form player in the women's game. Victory over Bucsa was the 2025 French Open winner's eighth straight-set WTA Tour-level win in a row. The fourth round is where Gauff's US Open challenge ended in the previous two editions, and she admitted that she struggled to handle the pressure last year. But in recovering from a 3-1 deficit in the first set, and producing an immediate response to being broken to love in the second, Gauff demonstrated she is better placed to cope with that this time. "I feel like I'm used to getting to the second week now. I woke up today and I was like 'oh we're already in round three'," Gauff said. "There's expectations, being American, and I want to do well in front of the fans. "Last year, I put so much pressure on myself. I'm enjoying the experience out here." I got really scared - Keys Keys appeared on course for a first fourth-round appearance at her home slam since 2023 after taking a commanding third set lead against Olympic champion Zheng. But the 2025 Australian Open winner would miss a match point and lose each of the final seven games in a 1-6 7-6 (7-3) 7-5 loss that stunned the crowd. The 31-year-old Keys said she felt as though she "couldn't play tennis anymore" in the final set. "I obviously got off to a really good lead, and then I got really scared, like I couldn't swing [the racquet]," Keys said. "I felt like I couldn't play tennis anymore. It just felt like it was a much bigger deal than just playing a tennis match all of a sudden." Keys, who lost the 2017 US Open final to fellow American Sloane Stephens, went out in the fourth round at the other three majors in 2026. "I feel like I've been struggling for a while now. I'm going to have to make some sort of changes," Keys said. "I just kind of keep putting it off because that's how the tennis world works. It's just to the point where I actually need to do something about it." Anisimova, beaten by world number one Aryna Sabalenka in last year's US Open final, lost in straight sets to Russian-born Austrian 24th seed Anastasia Potapova. The 25-year-old was visibly frustrated with herself throughout the contest, losing her serve twice in the first set and four times in a topsy-turvy second. Related topics - Published28 August

entry.title: Fritz and Cobolli shocked as men's seeds tumble
entry.body: Fritz and Cobolli shocked as men's seeds tumble - Published Taylor Fritz was unable to explain how he let a two-set lead slip against Francisco Cerundolo as he became one of six top-10 seeds to be eliminated from the men's draw in the first week of the US Open. The American ninth seed was in complete control and went an early break up in the third set, only for Argentina's Cerundolo to produce a shock 3-6 4-6 6-3 6-4 6-4 win to reach the fourth round. Less than an hour later, fifth seed Flavio Cobolli of Italy fell to a 7-6 (7-4) 3-6 0-6 3-6 defeat by Belgium's Alexander Blockx, opening up the men's draw even further. "I don't even know what to say," Fritz said. "I don't really want to talk to anybody, see anybody. "I need to get out for a couple days and then get back to work. I don't know how I let that happen today." Cerundolo and 28th seed Blockx will now meet in the fourth round with a place in the quarter-finals up for grabs. How the seeds have fallen This year's biggest shock at Flushing Meadows was also the first, as Novak Djokovic was beaten by Argentina's Mariano Navone on the opening day's play. Fourth seed Djokovic was eyeing an historic 25th Grand Slam title but was left in tears after a five-set loss to the world number 49. Next to go was 10th seed Arthur Fils. The Frenchman was another first-round casualty as he went down in four sets against former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas of Greece. The highest seed ousted thus far is Canada's Felix Auger-Aliassime, the third seed, who lost to Karen Khachanov in round two, the same stage at which sixth seed Alex de Minaur was beaten. Those exits looked to have cleared the way for Fritz and Cobolli to go deep into the tournament, but it was an opportunity neither were able to take. For Fritz, a finalist at Flushing Meadows in 2024, the frustration is all the greater at his home Slam. He was bidding to become the fifth American through to the fourth round at this year's tournament. With no Jannik Sinner to contend with and Carlos Alcaraz only recently returned from a wrist injury, excitement was growing that, 23 years on from Andy Roddick's US Open triumph, there may finally be another home winner in the men's singles. That chance persists - but Fritz will know he has let a golden opportunity slip. - Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory - Published4 hours ago - Gauff wins but mixed fortunes for home hopes at US Open - Published3 minutes ago Cobolli exit clears path for Zverev The chance of a maiden Grand Slam title has also escaped Cobolli for another few months after his capitulation against Blockx. Having edged the first set on a tie-break, the Italian lost his way and after surrendering the third set to love in just 20 minutes, could not recover. "I think my energy was a little bit lower than the other days," he said. "I feel a little bit more tight and maybe more tired." Cobolli admitted Blockx deserved the win and would support him in the next round. "Alex is very good guy outside the court. He deserved to win, and he won," he added. Defeats for Cobolli and Fritz mean that apart from top seed Alexander Zverev, only two top-20 players remain in the top half of the draw in 14th seed Learner Tien and 17th seed Jakub Mensik - and they play one another on Friday. It means Zverev could feasibly reach the final without playing a top-10 player and will not have to face anyone in the top 20 before the semis. In the men's doubles, British pair Arthur Fery and Joshua Paris progressed with a 6-4 5-7 6-4 win over Anirudh Chandrasekar of India and Ivan Liutarevich of Belarus. Britain's Neal Skupski and American partner Christian Harrison, the fifth seeds, also advanced as they beat French duo Arthur Reymond and Luca Sanchez 6-0 7-6 (7-3). But there was disappointment for David Stevenson and Marcus Willis as they lost 5-7 7-6 (7-2) 6-3 to France's 11th seeds Sadio Doumbia and Fabien Reboul. Related topics - Published28 August
entry.summary: Taylor Fritz and Flavio Cobolli lose in the third round as six top-10 seeds are knocked out of the men's singles in the first week at the US Open.

entry.title: US Open 2026 results: Zheng Qinwen beats Madison Keys from match point down to reach fourth round - BBC
entry.body: Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory - Published Zheng Qinwen described her US Open third-round comeback win over Madison Keys as a "very dramatic match" - but that is somewhat of an understatement. The Olympic champion, who had to come through qualifying to reach the main draw, found herself 5-0 and match point down in the third set against Keys. But Zheng held firm and reeled off seven games in a row to secure a remarkable 1-6 7-6 (7-3) 7-5 victory over the 22nd seed and crowd favourite. Keys, who won the 2025 Australian Open, appeared to be cruising towards a commanding victory after wrapping up the opening set in just 23 minutes. But Zheng, who is rebuilding her career after undergoing elbow surgery last year, rallied, clinching it on a tie-break before snatching victory from the jaws of defeat against the American. Zheng threw herself to the floor in relief and reflected afterwards on a difficult 12 months in which she has questioned if she will rediscover her form. "Finally, a bit of luck is on my side," the 23-year-old said. "I am just telling myself ever give up. Somehow, little by little, it's just happened. "Tennis sometimes feels like rollercoaster. You see many times people have a match point, but at the end we made a comeback." The Chinese star is the first qualifier to reach the women's fourth round at the US Open since Britain's Emma Raducanu, who went on to win the 2021 title. 'I forgot how to compete' - but Zheng rises again Three months ago, Zheng could not hold back her tears in a news conference after a first-round exit at the French Open. It was her first Grand Slam since undergoing surgery in July 2025 to correct a chronic injury caused by small pieces of bone floating in the elbow. The injury came after a breakthrough 2024 where she reached the Australian Open final, won Olympic gold and made the US Open quarter-finals. She had also enjoyed a promising start to 2025 before injury struck, advancing to the last eight at Roland Garros and climbing to a career-high of fourth in the world rankings. It was understandable, therefore, why Zheng found a first-round defeat in Paris this year difficult to take - even if it was to eventual runner-up Maja Chwalinska after nine months on the sidelines. Her ranking dropped as low as 160 and she had to contest a Grand Slam qualifying event for the first time in four years. "After coming back from injury I felt I lost the energy and I forgot how to compete," she said. Zheng seems to have recaptured some of her best form, having been taken to three sets in four of her six matches in New York so far. She did not meet criteria for a protected ranking - for which players can apply if they are out injured for at least six months - because she made an early comeback to play her home tournament in Beijing in October 2025. That meant she had to come through qualifying - something she found difficult to accept. "I was even crying after I won the third match to reach the main draw," Zheng said. "The main draw is just the beginning where all the players start. That was my beginning before. "I fight so hard just to start like everyone else. For me, that was really not easy." Her composure was on display against Keys - especially at 5-4 0-15 down, when she was forced to stop her service motion after a baby started crying in the crowd. "If it's adult, probably I will look at him very hard or start to speak, but it's just a baby," Zheng joked. "I can't do anything, you know? It's just a baby." Zheng went on to win the next four points to level the tie - and the rest was history. Related topics - Published4 hours ago - PublishedJust now

entry.title: 'One of the best' - boxing world reacts to Taylor's farewell win
entry.body: 'One of the best' - boxing world reacts to Taylor's farewell win - Published Some of the biggest names in women's boxing have paid tribute to Katie Taylor after the Irish great ended her career with victory over Flora Pili at Croke Park. Unified lightweight champion Caroline Dubois called Taylor "one of the best to ever do it", while Claressa Shields said the 40-year-old deserved to "ride off into the sunset". Taylor beat Pili on points in Dublin to become undisputed light-welterweight champion and retires with 26 wins from 27 professional contests, Olympic gold and three undisputed title triumphs across two divisions. "Thank you so much for paving the way," Londoner Dubois wrote on X. "Wishing you happiness, success and joy for this next season." Taylor was sharper throughout, repeatedly beating the Frenchwoman to the punch before finishing with one final burst of combinations as the crowd rose to its feet. American Shields - the self-proclaimed Greatest Woman of All Time - added: "Congrats Katie. Now ride off into the sunset. You deserve it all." Super-featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner described Taylor as "a trailblazer who helped set the stage for all of us". "What a legacy," she wrote. "It's been a privilege watching your journey from the beginning." 'There will never be another one like her' Taylor's farewell unfolded in front of more than 80,000 fans in Dublin, with Westlife performing before the main event and Croke Park providing a fitting backdrop to her final night. Former world champion Carl Frampton said Taylor's relationship with the Irish public was unlike anything else in boxing. "You can tell that she doesn't enjoy doing stuff in front of the media, but she still has this adulation from everybody," the Northern Irishman said. "Katie Taylor is different, she's special and there will never be another one like her." Former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew described the occasion as one of the most remarkable exits the sport had seen. "I don't think in all of my years of watching this game, I have seen an exit as beautiful, amazing and fitting," he said. "She has just retired as the greatest champion ever. I have never seen a fighter leave as an undisputed champion on their own terms." Former world champion Barry Jones picked out the final 20 seconds, when Taylor produced the kind of rapid combinations which defined so many of her biggest fights. "That's what you really remember about her," he said on the Dazn broadcast. "Those rallies of big punches, combinations and that's how she finished her last fight." American Mikaela Mayer - who was also ringside - was struck by the final image of Taylor placing her gloves in the centre of the ring. "I was sitting there watching her put her gloves in the centre of the ring and it's like a story," she said. Taylor had long dreamed of fighting at Croke Park and had made clear she wanted the stadium to stage the final chapter of her career. Bellew said there was "no way" Taylor would return to boxing, although he could see her remaining involved by mentoring younger fighters. "She will always be there to give her advice, speak to her and help her," he said. "But ultimately she will sail off into the sunset and who could possibly deserve it more." entry.title: Marmol ejected after rookie Rincon told to straighten hat out - MLB.com
entry.body: DENVER -- Cardinals manager Oliver Marmol was ejected from Friday’s series-opening 7-6 victory over the Rockies after arguing with home-plate umpire Doug Eddings regarding comments the umpire made to rookie Hancel Rincon about the way he was wearing his cap. Rincon was making his Major League debut in the sixth inning of a game the Cardinals led 4-1. According to Eddings, one of the Rockies batters asked about the tilt of Rincon’s cap. Eddings did not specify which batter raised the issue. “The batter said, ‘Hey, can he wear his hat like that?’” Eddings recounted after the game. “I really didn't know, but it was really, really crooked. I asked the catcher to tell him to straighten his hat out, and the pitcher did. Nobody said anything until he gave up a couple runs.” Reporters from the St. Louis Post-Dispatch and MLB.com, who spoke to Eddings after the game, initially reported the issue was raised during Hunter Goodman’s at-bat to lead off the inning, but Goodman clarified on Saturday that he did not raise the issue with Geddings and had no problem with Rincon or his cap. Video from the game indicates that the exchange between Eddings, catcher Leo Bernal and Rincon did not take place during Goodman’s at-bat. Rincon said the comment didn’t distract him from his debut and that he didn’t argue with Eddings about his comment. “I had no idea why he told me to do it,” Rincon said through an interpreter. “It's fine.” Rincon retired Goodman on a liner to second, then yielded a triple to TJ Rumfield, an inside-the-park home run to Cole Carrigg and a single to Connor Norby before Marmol went to Justin Bruihl to complete the inning, leaving starting pitcher Andre Pallante with a no-decision after five innings of one-run ball in his return from the injured list. Marmol continued to engage with Eddings after the pitching change, earning a pitch clock violation for Bruihl and, ultimately, an ejection for Marmol, his fourth of the season. “I had an issue with Doug,” Marmol said, emphasizing that he wasn’t arguing about a challenge made on Rumfield’s triple. He took it upon himself to tell our rookie pitcher the kid's ‘not going to wear his hat on my field that way.’ You got Dontrelle Willis, CC Sabathia, Pedro Strop -- plenty of guys that have worn it way more tilted. I have an issue with that. That's just a power-hungry move, in my opinion." Eddings admitted that Rincon wasn’t breaking a rule, but he maintained it was appropriate for him to give what Marmol called “a directive,” as opposed to advice. “It's not [a rule],” Eddings said. “I guess it's a little unwritten rule. They can't wear [their cap] backwards like a catcher. If it's a distraction, like anything on the field, like a glove or something, and someone makes you aware of it, then you kind of address that.” The Cardinals trailed until the ninth inning, when Iván Herrera took advantage of a throwing error in the previous at-bat and knocked a Statcast-projected 430-foot homer to center for the final score of 7-6.
entry.summary: Marmol ejected after rookie Rincon told to straighten hat out MLB.com Ump's issue with rookie's cap irked Cardinals. The Bulldogs pulled off a 63-56 win to kickstart the two school’s series. 𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐓𝐡𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐝𝐚𝐲: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞 𝐰𝐞 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐞 🎥 On October 11, 2014, The Bulldogs pulled off a thrilling 63-56 double overtime win over the 49ers in an instant classic at Johnson Hagood Stadium! 📼… pic.twitter.com/vzsrswWRSx Auburn makes two-point stand to defeat Baylor Former South Florida coach Alex Golesh delivered a Week 1 win for Auburn fans, defeating Baylor 17-16, in a finish that embodied the expression 'game of inches'. Baylor quarterback DJ Lagway led a 14-play, 70-yard touchdown drive, leaving just nine seconds on the clock in the fourth. But Baylor coach Dave Aranda opted to go for the win. Lagway rolled out to the right, but the pass was slightly inside, giving time for Auburn's Eric Winters to fly in and stuff tight end Matthew Klopfenstein just inches short of the goal line. AUBURN ESCAPES BAYLOR BY STOPPING THE 2-POINT ATTEMPT 🔥 UNBELIEVABLE FINISH. pic.twitter.com/G42ljb5sPx Lagway finished 27-of-54 for 333 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. A BIG stop for Oregon pic.twitter.com/T7HcRIPfRa Ducks quarterback Dante Moore had a poster performance, going 28-of-37 and finishing the game with 388 yards for three touchdowns. Dan Lanning's squad previously escaped Boise in a Week 2 matchup in 2024 with Oregon pulling out a 37-34 win. Boise State went on to make the playoffs that year as the No. 3 seed and Mountain West champion. Top performances entering night games We’d like to say thank you to Week 1 of the college football season thus far. There’s a lot that makes this sport so great, but stats like these are what keep us saying, “Wow. That’s insane.” Let’s unpack a few of today’s craziest numbers as the afternoon winds down. - Quarterback Mason Heintschel rounded out Pitt’s 59-14 win over Miami (OH) with 453 yards and seven (yes, seven) touchdowns, going 31-of-41. He's the first ACC signal caller since at least 1995 with over 450 passing yards and more than seven TDs. - Army ran the ball 57 times against Bryant, recording 569 rushing yards — the most rushing yards in a game by an FBS team since 2022. Hines carried the ball 26 times, rushing for 250 yards. Tarleton State notched its second win over an FBS team in two years with a 20-13 victory over Bowling Green. We still have plenty of action on the board tonight. Follow along here for more updates from Week 1. Perfect Pass 🤌😮💨 That's a career-high fifth TD pass for @mason_heinch06, this one to @CensereLee! 📺 @TheCW_Sports Pitt 45, Miami (OH) 14 pic.twitter.com/pO23Jpko7r Ranked teams roll in early games We’re four hours deep into Week 1 action, and so far, the preseason ranked teams are holding their expectations. 6 Indiana cruise with new-look offense Curt Cignetti’s new quarterback Josh Hoover has big shoes to fill following Fernando Mendoza’s Heisman season, but the TCU transfer left little to doubt in a 52-16 routing of North Texas. Hoover went 13-16 for 231 yards and four touchdowns in his debut, joining Mendoza as just the second Hoosier QB with four TDs and 80% completion in the past 30 years. But Hoosier-bred Charlie Becker led the receiving corps with 64 yards and two touchdown grabs. What a snag by Nick Marsh to put @IndianaFootball in front first 😳 pic.twitter.com/3DvAiBSlql — FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) September 5, 2026 Sayin-Smith kick off Heisman campaign with No. 1 Ohio State Yes, Jeremiah Smith still has one more season before he terrorizes NFL secondaries, and Ball State received the blow today as QB Julian Sayin and Smith connected for 151 yards and two touchdowns in a 56-3 win. Sayin completed 21 of 25 passes for 320 yards and three touchdowns before being pulled in the second half. The Buckeyes outgained the Cardinals 671-165 as Ryan Day’s squad turns its attention to No. THE best wide receiver in the country doing what he does best. @Jermiah_Smith1 | #GoBucks pic.twitter.com/9iQKN9LRvQ — Ohio State Football (@OhioStateFB) September 5, 2026 No. 18 Alabama runs past East Carolina With Ty Simpson’s departure to the NFL, Kalen Deboer settled on sophomore Keelon Russell under center. He immediately showed off his dual-threat abilities in the 48-10 win over the Pirates. Russell led the Tide with 86 yards on the ground and a touchdown, also throwing for 256 yards. All five of Alabama’s offensive touchdowns were on the ground. I mean, what are you supposed to do to stop Keelon Russell here? pic.twitter.com/NFOTbXC2hl — Gabe Burggraf (@GabeBurggraf) September 5, 2026 The Tide held ECU to only 22 rushing yards, allowing just 0.1 yards per attempt. Russell and company kick off their SEC campaign next Saturday on the road against Kentucky. FCS Tarleton State beats FBS Bowling Green We have our first FCS-over-FBS win of the season. Tarleton State took down Bowling Green, 20-13 on Saturday — the program's second such win in two years. Last year, the Texans beat Army 30-27. That means the they now have two wins in a row against the FBS. Tarleton State, which is ranked No. 5 in the AFCA FCS Coaches Poll, out-gained the Falcons 464 to 386 thanks to Tylan Hines' 250 rushing yards. QB Kaden Anderson also had a big day, passing for 206 yards and a pair of touchdowns. The Texans moved up from DII to FCS starting with the 2020-21 season. TEXANS STRIKE FIRST ⚡️ Tanner Schmidt hauls in his second touchdown on the year on a fade from Kaden Anderson! 7-0 Texans to start the game at Bowling Green pic.twitter.com/yyP7RITAwa Here's how we got a tie in college football today FINAL: Washburn 16, Colorado School of Mines 16. A DII football game ended in a tie. And it was one that kicked off in the morning. After lengthy discussion between officials and the two teams, Saturday's Washburn vs. Colorado School of Mines game was called with it 16-16 in OT, in line with NCAA rules on suspended games. The game kicked off at 9 a.m. local time in Topeka, Kan., to accommodate the Orediggers' travel plans and in hopes of finishing before the predicted field temperature rose past safety protocols. The game was originally scheduled for noon CT but then was moved to 7:05 before it settled on the 9 a.m. As noted by Colorado School of Mines — "the game was stopped due to an MIAA rule stipulating that any wet bulb temperature above 92.1 will cause a contest to be suspended until it falls to a safe temperature. entry.title: UFC Paris: Michael 'Venom' Page wins in underwhelming UFC farewell - BBC
entry.body: Fans boo as MVP wins in underwhelming UFC farewell - Published Michael 'Venom' Page's last fight on his UFC contract ended in an underwhelming win against Nursulton Ruziboev amid booing fans in Paris. London's Page, who is nicknamed 'MVP', landed a handful of eye-catching strikes during the contest but could not deliver the knockout that the fans craved as he won by unanimous decision. The 39-year-old's victory means all five of his wins in the UFC since joining in 2024 have come via decision. Page joined the UFC with a reputation as an innovative striker with a resume of highlight-reel knockouts, but admitted pre-fight he has underperformed since joining the organisation. Page said the fight with Uzbekistan's Ruziboev was "important to re-establish myself with the UFC", but he did not get the finish he wanted. Page, who arrived in the UFC over two years ago with 13 knockouts to his name, received a raucous ovation from the French crowd as he entered the octagon. Ruziboev controlled the majority of the first round on the ground before Page started to open up midway through the fight. He landed a kick to Ruziboev's knee which wobbled the 32-year-old, before smiling and showboating as he delivered a number of feints. Page delivered an overhead right and an elbow, but the explosive moments were few and far between as the crowd grew frustrated at a lack of action. Throughout the bout, Page landed only 12 significant strikes to Ruziboev's eight. Page has shown throughout his UFC career he is a master of movement and evasion, without having the finishing instinct that the most successful fighters possess. The fight against Ruziboev followed the same pattern, and although Page was awarded victory by the judges, his arm was raised after jeers from the crowd. With Page now a free agent, potential options for him if he does not re-sign with the UFC include joining the PFL or turning to boxing. In the main event, French-Moroccan Salahdine Parnasse earned a stunning first-round TKO win over Dan Hooker. Parnasse was making his UFC debut and delivered in front of a home crowd, landing a punishing kick to the body before dropping New Zealand's Hooker with a left hook. The 28-year-old followed with a flurry of punches as Hooker, ranked 12 in the lightweight division, shelled up on the floor, forcing the referee to wave off the contest. There was also victory for fellow Briton Kurtis Campbell, who submitted American Trevor Peek in the third round of their featherweight bout via a rear-naked choke. It was a return to winning ways for the 24-year-old Liverpudlian, who lost on his UFC debut to Danny Silva in March. Campbell's win extends his professional record to nine wins and one defeat. "I know my debut didn't go the way I wanted it to but I'm here to show I'm the real deal and the future is bright," said Campbell. Earlier on the card, London's Nathaniel Wood lost by unanimous decision to Moldova's Pavel Andrusca, bringing his four-fight win streak to an end. Andrusca, who was a late replacement after Wood's original opponent Mairon Santos withdrew 10 days prior to the fight, extended the unbeaten start to his career to nine. At UFC 322 on 3 October in Salt Lake City, it was announced Brazil's Natalia Silva will fight for the vacant flyweight title against China's Wang Cong. Former title holder Valentina Shevchenko has vacated the belt and is set to miss over a year with injury, according to the UFC. entry.title: Jones stuns Trump to set up final against Selby
entry.body: Jones stuns Trump to set up final against Selby - Published Jak Jones earned a surprise win against Judd Trump at the British Open and will face Mark Selby in the final. Jones produced breaks of 95 and 68 on the way to a 3-1 lead before Trump levelled the match at 3-3. However, Jones knocked in a 59 and a 52 to go 5-3 in front and, after England's Trump missed a green on the colours in a lengthy ninth frame, the Welshman secured victory. "I started off quite well before the interval and then after that I started missing a few, didn't I?" Jones, beaten finalist in the 2024 World Championship, told Channel 5. "I can't say I'm in this position a lot so it's a bit different for me compared to Judd." Meanwhile, Selby came through a hard-fought win against fellow Englishman Liam Highfield, who was playing in his first ranking event semi-final. Highfield took the opening frame before Selby levelled with an 85 and moved into a 3-2 lead. A 56 helped Highfield level at 3-3, but Selby took three frames in a row to secure a 6-3 victory and a place in his 40th ranking event final. "It was a tough match, Liam didn't make it easy for me at all," said Selby, who can climb from fourth to second in the rankings if he wins the title. I can't remember him playing a poor safety shot all the way through the match." He added: "To think, when I was starting out, a 16-year-old kid in 1999, if somebody had said I'd get to 40 ranking finals, I'd have said 'no chance'. I'd have been happy to get to just one or two."
entry.summary: Jak Jones earns a surprise win against Judd Trump at the British Open, and will face Mark Selby in the final.

entry.title: Humphries beats Greaves as Littler also wins
entry.body: Humphries beats Greaves as Littler also wins - Published Luke Humphries and Luke Littler came through their second round matches to progress at the Czech Open on the European Tour. Humphries ended the challenge of Beau Greaves, who had become the first woman to win a match on the European Tour with her first round win over Daryl Gurney. The world number two averaged nearly 109 as he beat the three-time women's World Matchplay champion 6-2 in Prague. "She's an amazing player, she pushed me all the way, it was a couple of bits towards the end of the match that got me through in the end," said Humphries, who will play Andrew Gilding in the third round. "She's just a great dart player. If I had lost today, I wouldn't have been disgraced, I would have lost to a really great dart player." World number one Littler had missed the last eight events on the European Tour and marked his return with a 6-4 victory against Germany's Niko Springer. Littler, who won the men's World Matchplay title in July but was beaten by Brendan Dolan in the semi-finals of a Players Championship event last month, had a 108.59 average in his win. "It's been a while since I've been to a European Tour," said Littler, who will next play Krzysztof Ratajski. I was 5-2 up and then suddenly it was 5-4 and he was right back in it. "I've just produced a 108 average, but when I was practising backstage I couldn't hit anything." Michael van Gerwen and Gian van Veen also reached the last 16 with respective wins against Mario Vandenbogaerde and Jeffrey de Graaf.
entry.summary: Luke Humphries and Luke Littler came through their second round matches to progress at the Czech Open on the European Tour.

entry.title: ‘The Debut’ Explodes at Telluride With Julianne Moore’s Gonzo, Career-Best Turn, Thanks to a Toolbelt, Unlit Cigarettes and a Faux Musical
entry.body: Jesse Eisenberg has made his most significant debut to date. There is a delicious irony at the center of “The Debut,” Eisenberg’s third feature as a director, which world premiered at the Telluride Film Festival: it is a film about a nobody who attacks a bit part as if it were the role of a lifetime — and it arrives as one of the fall’s genuine best picture contenders, ready to make Oscar darlings out of Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti. Rebecca Keagan of NBC News moderated the Q&A with Eisenberg, Moore and Giamatti. It was Giamatti’s first time seeing the film. Popular on Variety Call it Eisenberg’s “Black Swan” by way of “Whiplash” and “Waiting for Guffman,” the whole fever dream staged inside a faux musical and relocated to a New Jersey rec center. Moore plays Mona Friedman, a meek housewife who hasn’t sung in front of anyone since church choir and is unexpectedly cast in a community-theater production — then transforms into a zealous method actor willing to wage war over a marginal role. Giamatti is Jerry, the tyrannical director billed, without irony, as the biggest name in New Jersey community theater. It is funny, then feral, then unexpectedly moving and it confirms that the filmmaker who won Kieran Culkin an Oscar with “A Real Pain” knows exactly how to build a showcase around actors. A24 sets it for Dec. 11, a release date that signals a studio going long — and A24 knows this walk. Twice it has turned an unlikely film into a best picture champion: “Moonlight,” which stunned the favored “La La Land and “Everything Everywhere All at Once,” an absurdist multiverse comedy that had no business winning and won anyway. “The Debut” hands the studio a broad, playable contender with two of the most beloved actors alive at its center. Start with Moore, who has quietly become the film’s frontrunner-in-waiting. She is a five-time nominee with a single win — “Still Alice,” more than a decade ago — and Mona is the sort of tragicomic tour de force that reintroduces a great actor to voters who may have forgotten how much they owe her. She plays it balls to the wall, fearless in the way of Natalie Portman or Cate Blanchett at full tilt. On Telluride’s Saturday afternoon screening, she drew spontaneous applause in the middle of two separate scenes — the kind of response that tells you everything. A sixth nomination is automatic. The win is the question, and the recent past is on her side: the modern Academy has grown notably comfortable handing out second — and even third — acting Oscars. Anthony Hopkins for “The Father,” Emma Stone for “Poor Things” (Stone, tellingly, produces “The Debut”), with Frances McDormand and Sean Penn all tripling up in recent years. A second Moore statuette would surprise no one. Giamatti’s case is different, and in some ways sweeter, because he is chasing his first. One of the most admired actors of his generation has never won — the “Sideways” snub remains a scar on the branch’s record, and his leading turn in “The Holdovers” lost to the “Oppenheimer” juggernaut. As Jerry, he has the flashier, more quotable role: the monstrous mentor, the archetype that won J.K. Simmons an Oscar in “Whiplash” but with heart. He also gets what may be the film’s best line — “That’s where everyone wants to be … center stage.” His likeliest and most winnable lane is supporting, the very category Culkin swept for Eisenberg two years ago. Lightning tends to strike the same script twice. There is something lovely, too, in the pairing of this and “Elsinore” on the same mountain: the two biggest swings at Telluride this year are both love letters to acting itself. “The Debut” is less a musical than a savage comedy about one — a movie set in the world of an original show rather than a wall-to-wall songbook. Drew Daniels, fresh off “Anora,” shoots it; Emil Mosseri, an Oscar nominee for “Minari,” scores it; Bernadette Peters and Halle Bailey enrich an ensemble with real Broadway bona fides. Eisenberg, himself a screenplay nominee for “A Real Pain,” has written another original that plays far bigger than its logline. It has the bones of a lighthearted Tarantino picture spliced with the DNA of “Stranger Than Fiction” — and it arrived at Telluride with a résumé, then left with a possible frontrunner status. There are no small parts, the old theater adage goes, only small actors. “The Debut” turns the cliché into a thesis and dares you to disagree.

entry.title: Bad Bunny Wins Emmy for Super Bowl Halftime Show
entry.body: Bad Bunny has won his first Emmy for the Super Bowl Halftime Show. He won in the outstanding variety special (live) category. “The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny” took home a total of seven nominations, winning music direction, choreography, sound mixing, lighting design, technical direction/camerawork and directing. Bad Bunny and the event’s producers and directors pulled off what may have been the most intricate halftime extravaganza in Super Bowl history. Superstar guests included Lady Gaga and Ricky Martin, a real-life wedding and authentic business owners (including Los Angeles’ own Villa’s Tacos) among the set. Speaking about the performance, creative director Harriet Cuddeford previously told Variety, “The performance is celebrating normal people, and what it is to be human and love and have joy, and really appreciate one another. This was to show how much he values his community, to celebrate normal people on the world’s biggest stage, especially people who are of importance in Latino culture. He’s a very authentic person, Benito, and it’s about just being authentic and very real and very human.”

entry.title: Liam and Noel Gallagher Raise Fists and Electrify Venice as Oasis Doc Gets 8-Minute Standing Ovation
entry.body: Oasis mania hit Venice Film Festival on Saturday night as Liam and Noel Gallagher presented the world premiere of their highly anticipated documentary “Don’t Look Back in Anger.” The rock doc received an eight-minute standing ovation as the once-estranged brothers held hands and raised them triumphantly. Though the Gallaghers aren’t one for emotions, Noel at one point appeared to be wiping tears from his eyes while Liam hyped up the crowd. The atmosphere inside the Palazzo del Cinema was electric, with fans clamoring to get a photo, autograph or just a look at the iconic musicians. Before the screening, the brothers were greeted with cheers of “C’mon, boys!” and “Fight!” One fan even brought a Manchester City flag (their football club of choice) and flew it over the balcony. As the documentary rolled on, the rowdiness continued — attendees clapped after most of the live performances in the film and, as the audience sang along to “Champagne Supernova,” several were reduced to audible tears. During the actual standing ovation, the brothers — understandably new to the film festival world — looked like they had no idea what to do, with Liam eyeing his watch and mouthing, “Should we fuck off?” before creator Steven Knight seemingly convinced him to stay. But all hell broke loose when the Gallaghers descended into the crowd to sign autographs, turning the theater into a mild mosh pit as fans jockeyed for a selfie or signature. One thing’s for sure, this is likely to be the closest Venice Film Festival gets to a rock concert. Popular on Variety Earlier on the red carpet, Italian fans donned their best bucket hats and band merch, singing along to “Acquiesece” and “Wonderwall” as they waited for Liam and Noel to arrive. Ever the rock ‘n’ roll stars, when they finally did, it was through the cinema’s entrance instead of from a car at the start of the carpet, causing screams to erupt. The Gallaghers, known for their love of windbreakers and Fred Perry polos, dressed smartly for the occasion in all black (though still decidedly unfancy, with Liam layering a T-shirt underneath a blazer and Noel wearing a zip-up jacket). Oasis!” as the brothers signed autographs separately, before coming together to pose for photos — even holding hands and raising them up victoriously for one shot. Directed by Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace, the documentary “charts Liam and Noel Gallagher’s triumphant reunion tour, Oasis Live ‘25, one of the most anticipated rock ‘n’ roll comebacks of our time,” according to its official synopsis. The film, which premieres in theaters Sept. 11 before bowing on Disney+ later this year, boasts footage of the band both backstage and onstage as well as the first joint interview with often-feuding brothers Noel and Liam in over 20 years. The Oasis reunion tour last year marked the first time the Gallagher brothers had played together since 2009. Tickets for the tour sold out immediately and it went on to generate hundreds of millions of dollars across dates in the U.K., North America, South Korea, Japan, Australia, Argentina, Chile and Brazil. The success of Oasis Live ’25 — and the fact that the brothers are still getting along well enough to do press for their documentary together — has sparked rumors of a further Oasis tour, perhaps next year. Though the Gallaghers weren’t on hand at the film’s press conference earlier on Saturday to field questions, the band has posted several cryptic teasers on Instagram that have sent fans into detective mode. Adding to the speculation, Noel said in a recent interview on Talksport: “Let’s put it this way: there’s no football tournament on next year, so we’ve got to do something in the summer, right?”
