entry.title: ‘Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger’ Review: An Uncharacteristically Polite and Sentimental Portrait of a Raucous Band and Phenomenon
entry.body: The 2016 documentary “Supersonic,” focused on Oasis’ beginnings and incredibly fast rise to superstardom, made no mention of what was then the most salient fact about the Gallagher brothers: that from 2009, they were no longer on speaking terms. Ten years after that Asif Kapadia-produced doc, the concert film “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger” — world premiering at the Venice Film Festival —begins by placing the split front and center. After a short montage, which includes actual footage of the infamous Rock en Seine gig where the brothers never even made it to the stage, the film takes us right into the rehearsal room where, in the summer of 2025, the newly reunited band is set to practice together for six weeks. The question of whether sparks will fly between the siblings within this confined space hangs heavily in the air, and nifty editing plays up the anxiety around the project. But while some tension is palpable, sparks do not fly — or at least, filmmakers Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace (whose previous rock docs include 2010’s Grammy-nominated “No Distance Left to Run,” about Oasis’ old ’90s rivals Blur) do not choose to show them if they do. It is soon clear that “Don’t Look Back in Anger” is far from an unvarnished portrait of an often fraught relationship, let alone a tabloid-style collection of shocking anecdotes. Popular on Variety Although neither Noel nor Liam can help expressing themselves, in new on-camera interviews, in the candid manner that they always have, they remain not just on their best behavior, but also at what feels like a PR-trained remove. Their professional focus — the usually raucous Liam is described by a band member as being uncharacteristically “business” in rehearsals — is in step with a film whose attempts to conceal its obvious financial raison d’etre often feel absurd and tacked-on. With the two brothers on somewhat guarded form, offering little insight into their own thoughts or emotions throughout this experience, the film dedicates a significant portion of its two-hour runtime to the fans. “Don’t Look Back in Anger” might have benefited from the hindsight of a few more years and constructed a compelling argument about what Oasis meant in 2025, especially in the U.K. The tour seemed the latest and most spectacular sign of a society-wide nostalgia for the 1990s, responding perhaps to a series of national disasters (Brexit, Covid-19, rapidly succeeding prime ministers), and occurring in the middle of a wave of national pride and hope (the soccer) that was itself shoring up against decidedly less positive attitudes (the rise of right-wing politicians and policies). All this, compared to what Oasis meant at its peak in 1996, would make for a fascinating film that could also enshrine the band’s significance more successfully than yet another montage of newspaper headlines or references to album sales. As it is, the film only briefly and somewhat ironically touches on those world events that might explain why the 2025 tour was such a phenomenon. Over a rapid-fire montage showing footage of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, Keir Starmer, online videos of robots falling over, and other more-or-less severe indignities, Liam declares, “When Oasis split up, everything went to shit.” He continues, “People, more than ever now, they want to escape.” This idea that Oasis’s music provides a form of escape or release is entirely supported by the plentiful footage of concert-goers included in the film. Shouting out the lyrics like their lives depend on it, clutching at their loved ones, crying, even praying, and often in a state of apparent inebriation, these men and women are a far cry from the dreaded, zombie-like GenZ crowds that have frustrated countless acts in recent years — even though most of the fans seen in the film are under 30. This enthusiasm could be partly explained by the band’s unexpected reunion, but brief inserts of footage from Oasis’ triumphant shows at Knebworth in 1996 suggest that the Mancunian band engenders a type of fandom of a particularly feverish kind. The film puts it plainly in a sequence showing police security gathered ahead of the first reunion gig, as the chief of police tells the others that fans are expected to have “a herd mentality similar to that of football crowds.” It seems an odd choice, then, for the film to go in a less visceral and more sentimental direction. The impressive concert footage and appropriately very loud sound design (by “The Zone of Interest” Oscar winner Tarn Willers and James Mather) showcases big chunks of songs at their best, but they are frequently interrupted either by platitudes from the brothers which fans have surely heard before, or by brief tangents centered on fans from around the world. A woman in Brazil has named her dog after guitarist Paul “Bonehead” Arthurs; two female divers in South Korea talk about their friendship and the song “Acquiesce.” The most awkward if well-meaning inclusion is a survivor of the 2017 Manchester Arena attack which took place during an Ariana Grande concert. The young girl describes struggling with survivor’s guilt at the time, and finding solace in hearing Noel’s iconic ballad “Don’t Look Back in Anger” at a vigil; she is later seen singing along to the song at one of the reunion shows. Such attempts to touch on the highly personal connections people have to Oasis’s music feel clumsy and forced, especially when juxtaposed with the brothers’ rather anonymous comments. The film’s generally po-faced attitude as a whole seems an odd fit for the Gallaghers. It is difficult to imagine them not responding with a barb of some kind to the footage of an actual sermon. The priest likens the concert crowds to a pilgrimage, and quotes Matthew 18:21 (“Lord, how many times must I forgive my brother?”) before claiming that the people have come not so much for the music as “for the reconciliation between two brothers.” The somewhat bombastic approach of screenwriter and “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight, who created and wrote the doc, has been successful elsewhere, but feels at odds with the band’s ethos here. These stabs at earnestness do nothing to diminish the feeling of the concert film being little more than a cash grab. Likewise, the repeated point about Oasis’ working-class origins, while true, comes across as another attempt at striking a sentimental chord — in a way that feels anathema to Oasis. In a context where the price of concert tickets today excludes working-class fans from attending shows at all, it feels doubly insincere. It did not have to be this way. In one throwaway moment in the film, as Liam asks audiences to turn around and lock arms with the people around them, he refers to the people in the cheap seats, before adding, “Actually there are no cheap seats, sorry about that.” No Oasis fan would reproach the band for making a lot of money on their tour; in fact, there is no doubt that they would have cherished the chance to hear the two brothers bragging again together about how rich and successful they are, just like they used to do. “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger” should be of interest to fans who missed the 2025 tour or are seeking to relive some of its emotion. But its polite treatment of such a momentous event strips it of some of the specificity and intensity that are no doubt behind the band’s continued popularity.

entry.title: ‘Evil Dead’ star Bruce Campbell says he has five years to live after cancer diagnosis - NBC News
entry.body: Actor Bruce Campbell said he has five years to live amid treatment for cancer. Speaking on an episode of “The Adam Carolla Show” released Thursday, the actor — best known for his roles in “The Evil Dead” horror franchise — said he has “give or take” five years left. “I’ve decided though, pretty specifically, to live with it, not die from it,” he said. “The cancer rabbit hole is enormous. You can go into focus groups of 10,000 guys who have exactly what you have. I won’t touch it with a 10-foot pole.” Campbell, 67, declined to say what type of cancer he has. He announced his diagnosis in March, saying he had a “treatable” but not “curable” type of cancer. “I apologize if that’s a shock — it was to me too,” he wrote in a post on X at the time. “The good news is, I’m not gonna go into any more detail. I’m posting this, because professionally, a few things will have to change — appearances and cons and work in general need to take a back seat to treatment.” Campbell appeared on the podcast to promote “Ernie & Emma,” an independent film he wrote, directed, produced and stars in. I got a movie to promote. And when I promote this movie, I have nothing. I’m free and clear when I promote this movie mentally,” he said. “You have to make this decision of, ‘Well, OK, but do I have to stop everything that I’m doing because of this?’ Well, no.” “It’s not just, you don’t die for cancer,” he added. “You die from what cancer does to you.”

entry.body: There is a bigger story underneath, too. “La Bola Negra” is a Spanish-language epic Netflix is pushing to the front of the field and Cruz has long been the international face Academy voters know best, and this season she sits at the center of a Spanish-language surge pressing into the awards conversation on its own terms as a cultural dimension her résumé alone never carried. And then we have the question about the second Oscar itself. Cruz has already done what most actors spend a career chasing when she won the Oscar in 2009. However, there was a bit of an asterisk many felt since Kate Winslet, who had swept the circuit for “The Reader,” was shockingly moved to lead by the Academy where she ultimately won. Wouldn’t it be great to do a proper seasonal long coronation on one of the most astounding and talented international performers?
entry.summary: Penélope Cruz became an Oscar winner when 2008’s “Vicky Cristina Barcelona” made her the first Spanish actress to win an acting Oscar. Seventeen years later, she is not chasing a second statuette so much as choosing which vehicle to ride to the ceremony — because this season she has three. The biggest of the three […]

entry.title: Taylor Swift Says She Tried to Channel Randy Newman on ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’
entry.body: Taylor Swift Says She Tried to Channel Randy Newman on ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’ Taylor Swift didn’t take the opportunity to write a song for the Toy Story 5 soundtrack lightly. In June, the superstar made her big country music return with the evocative single. “It really hit me the weight of this, how lucky we were to get to take up what Randy Newman has created and and continue that legacy,” Swift said on American Country Countdown with Ryan Fox, referring to the country single “I Knew It, I Knew You,”which she and Jack Antonoff wrote for the film. “I just thought we’re gonna take these beautiful tapestries of musical art he’s created brushstroke by brushstroke, and we’re gonna try to create something that would go in that collection.” Swift continued: “I’m a huge Randy Newman fan, so is Jack. Randy tends to go to really different kind of chord progressions and has very different musical sensibilities than I do. So we try to channel that, you know, what would Randy do.” The singer-songwriter joined Newman onstage at the Toy Story 5 premiere in June and performed the acclaimed composer’s “You’ve Got a Friend in Me.” Newman took over the keys as the pair swapped vocals, his voice as tender and warm as ever. Y’all Access with Kelly Sutton also aired an audio message from Swift, where she further discussed the wistful single. The superstar’s rare appearance across country radio comes after she returned to the genre with “I Knew It, I Knew You,” and has been cozying up to country radio once more. Before the release of the single, Swift reportedly met with a bunch of country radio programmers to preview the song. It may have just been industry-level hobnobbing, but it’s hard to imagine it was required in this situation. As RJ Curtis, executive director of Country Radio Broadcasters Inc., told Rolling Stone earlier this year, “I have said for a while now that given the right song, country radio will support her again and welcome her back with open arms, and it looks like she delivered in a huge way.” Notably, “I Knew It, I Knew You” was an immediate hit on country radio. It topped the Hot Country Songs chart and reached Number Eight on the Country Airplay chart. (And hit Number One on the Billboard Hot 100.) It even made history when it became the first song by a woman to close out the panel on impact, meaning, every country radio station reporting to Mediabase signed on to play the song in the first week. In a note shared in the industry trade Country Aircheck, Swift wrote, “Man, it’s been a while! Thank you for making history with me.
entry.summary: The singer-songwriter discussed her Toy Story 5 song in rare appearance across three country radio stations

entry.title: ‘Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes’ Review: The Legendary Rocker Gets a Lively Doc That Asks: Who Are You? And Then Doesn’t Fully Answer It
entry.body: Every rock god has his ultimate gesture of power, and for Pete Townshend it was not the way he liked to smash his guitar (though that came close). No, the quintessential Townshend power sign was his giant circular windmill strum, arm outstretched and twirling, gathering centrifugal force to slam that pick up through the guitar strings, creating the loudest chord humanly possible. The impulse behind that gesture — the destructive fury of it — is the same one that gave rise to Led Zeppelin and punk. And you get to see Townshend do it a bunch of times in Frank Marshall and Nigel Sinclair’s “Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes,” the lively and somewhat scattered documentary that just premiered at Telluride. As music docs go, it’s a serviceable rock ride, with plenty of great archival footage that’s never been seen before. (It’s been culled from long-lost 16mm reels shot at Holmhurst Manor in 1972, as well as Townshend’s home movies and outtakes from the Who’s 1970 Isle of Wight performance.) But the power-chord side of Townshend ends up taking something of a back seat in “Behind Blue Eyes.” The movie is more interested in his anguished moody poetic side, the one that created the great rock opera “Tommy” (a work nearly as pivotal as “Sgt. Pepper,” and one built around Townshend’s childhood trauma), as well as his desire to expand beyond it by making rock over into something bigger, bolder, more confessionally grandiose. Popular on Variety Townshend was a Mod who grew up into a rock intellectual who still talked like a bloke. He’s incredibly thoughtful, and always has been, but he could also be something of a doomy drama queen. He led the early Who with burn-it-all-down ferocity, yet was always concerned about the effects of rock, wanting it to stay positive. The film sketches in how Townshend got his start in art school, and in his case it really stuck. He wanted rock to be an art form. He swiped the idea of guitar-smashing from films he was shown as a student of avant-garde classical musicians destroying pianos. His days with the Who began as a lark (he never planned to make a career of it), but the group became a draw in West London. There’s a great clip of them from 1965 playing “I Can’t Explain,” with its tight chords that were so ’50s yet so new, as Townshend bops out to it. It’s strange, though, that “Behind Blue Eyes” skips over the epochal moment of “My Generation,” one of the 10 most seismic and influential songs in the history of rock ‘n’ roll. When punk finally came along, the movie talks about how Townshend, who totally dug the punk scene, tried to cozy up to Johnny Rotten and got nowhere. It notes how much influence the Who had on punk — but that would be “My Generation,” which the film never got around to mentioning! Other jarring omissions: We’re informed that Keith Moon, the Who’s thrash genius of a drummer, died of a drug overdose (the drug was chlomethiazole, a sedative prescribed to alleviate the symptoms of alcohol withdrawal), but the movie never says a word about his drinking. (He might have been the biggest drinker in the history of rock.) And while we’re told that Townshend was dead set against making a movie of “Tommy,” the film leaves out the impact of Ken Russell’s opulently feverish 1975 big-screen version. There’s already a definitive movie about the Who, the formative rock doc “The Kids Are Alright” (1979), so Marshall and Sinclair may have felt that they could sort of skip through the band’s career. Yet “Behind Blue Eyes,” though it is a film about Townshend, remains very, very Who centered. Townshend, who’s 81 now, sits for an extended interview, wearing a red wool cap over his bald head. He is open and circumspect, with a disarming gentleness. He tells the Who’s story — as does Roger Daltrey, who sat down for the filmmakers — with a ripe feeling for the heights they scaled and a wistful sense of how far away the feuds and valleys now seem. “Behind Blue Eyes” opens, quite dramatically, on the crisis Townshend was going through after “Tommy” became a majestic success. Townshend had evolved his whole idea for a rock opera out of the two years, starting at age four, when he was abandoned by his parents and sent to live with his sexually debauched grandmother. He was never abused, but he says he was so distraught that he literally tuned out reality; he became that “deaf, dumb and blind kid.” Townshend composed and recorded the music for “Tommy” at home (in demos that were then built on in the studio). The band, at that point, had become entirely his. (He says the other three band members just wanted to party and sleep around.) But once “Tommy” changed the game for the Who, how could they top it? In films from the time, we see the fear frozen onto Townshend’s face. The Holmhurst Manor footage shows the members of the Who sitting around the Jacobean country house in East Sussex that was purchased by Roger Daltrey in 1970 (it was one of those aristocratic estates that noise-making British bands of the ’70s loved to record in), hashing out where they were going to go next. Because they had no idea. And we see the chaos they were feeling. Success had left them stranded, creatively, the same way that U2 were before they pulled themselves together to go in a new direction and make “Achtung Baby!” We also see how testy and difficult Townshend could be. That can happen when you’re the leader who doesn’t know where to lead. Watching this footage, I kept wishing that someone had made a Townshend biopic 30 years ago starring the young Ralph Fiennes. But, of course, the Who pulled through and found a new level of sonic triumph. I’ve often gone easy on the hagiographic side of music docs, and the reason is simple: While I prefer to get the full picture, if a movie plays down the dark side of an artist, but captures that artist’s music and career with vibrant appreciation, that can be enough to make an enlightening and captivating film. But “Behind Blue Eyes” may be a special case. The movie centers itself on Pete Townshend’s contradictions, his growing pains, his turmoil, and his complexity as a human being and rock artist. But given where it sets the bar, there’s too much left out. We learn a great deal about Townshend’s struggle to make “Lifehouse,” an unfinished science-fiction rock opera that he became obsessed with to the point that it starts to sound like something out of “Spinal Tap.” But we learn virtually nothing about Townshend’s close relationships, notably his two marriages. In 1980, when “Rough Boys,” his first solo single, was released, Townshend gave interviews acknowledging that he had, for a time, led a gay existence. Why isn’t that in the movie? And though we hear the gritty addiction details of Townshend’s dark period (when he’d become a junkie and was, by his own description, drinking three bottles of Cognac a day), what I wanted from the documentary wasn’t a bottoming-out-and-getting-sober narrative. I wanted the movie, and Townshend himself, to go deeper into why he descended into addiction. As a rock biography, “Behind Blue Eyes” is “exploratory” yet fuzzy. It’s not as riveting a portrait of the Who as “The Kids Are Alright” was (though there’s consistently great stuff in it), and for all its confessional aura it doesn’t leave you feeling that you truly know and understand Pete Townshend. It’s more like you’ve glimpsed him around the edges, without quite touching the bad man, or the sad man, behind blue eyes.
entry.summary: The film centers itself on Pete Townshend’s contradictions, his growing pains, his turmoil, and his complexity as a human being and rock artist. And that’s all good. But given where it sets the bar, there’s too much that's left out.

entry.title: Scoop: Republican midterms convention speakers revealed
entry.body: President Trump and his top allies will share the stage with Republican candidates in some of the nation's most competitive races at next week's GOP midterm convention in Dallas, according to a preliminary list of speakers obtained by Axios. Why it matters: The lineup underscores a central purpose of the convention: firing up Trump voters and getting them to turn out in November, even though the president isn't on the ballot. Driving the news: Trump will speak both nights of the Sept. 9-10 convention, while Vice President Vance will deliver a keynote address on the second night. The lineup also includes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Donald Trump Jr. House Speaker Mike Johnson, Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso and National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Tim Scott are among the congressional leaders who will appear. One name that is notably absent from the list is Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who Trump has attacked for not doing more to pass election security legislation. But Thune is scheduled to be in Dallas next week for fundraising, and organizers say they are still adding names to the list. Republicans in some of the toughest races aren't attending, including Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and former Sen. John Sununu in New Hampshire. Zoom out: Republicans will use the convention to mobilize Trump voters, who party strategists worry will be less inclined to turn out than they were two years ago. Much of the two-day event will be focused on branding Democrats as far-outside-the-mainstream socialists. Zoom in: The convention will put Trump onstage alongside Republicans running in many of the races that will determine control of Congress. Senate candidates include Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, Texas Republican Ken Paxton, Michigan Republican Mike Rogers, North Carolina Republican Michael Whatley and Georgia Rep. Mike Collins. Trump won all five states in 2024, though all of them are competitive this year. On the House side, New York Rep. Mike Lawler and Pennsylvania Reps. Rob Bresnahan and Ryan Mackenzie are among the vulnerable incumbents slated to speak, along with Wisconsin Rep. Derrick Van Orden. Lawler is the only House candidate on the roster running in a district Kamala Harris carried in 2024. Yes, but: Appearing at the convention isn't without risk for Republicans in tight races. Democrats are likely to portray them as closely aligned with Trump, whose approval rating was in the 30s in several recent polls. By the numbers: About 100 Republican lawmakers and candidates are expected to attend the convention, either as speakers or in the audience. A number of non-politicians will also address the convention. entry.title: TV presenter among 11 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case - BBC
entry.body: TV presenter among 11 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case Egyptian television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people have been sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drugs charges. According to state-owned al-Ahram newspaper, they were part of a criminal gang which imported ingredients used to make drugs with the intent of selling them. They also had illegal firearms and munitions. Khalifa, 39, is best known for her TV programme Mission Impossible which dealt with crime issues. She has denied the charges. The verdict - which can be appealed against - was first announced last month. However, it was only confirmed a month later after the court obtained a religious opinion from the grand mufti of Egypt - a legal requirement in death sentence cases. During the trial, the court heard that authorities had seized more than 750kg (1,653lbs) of narcotics and the imported raw materials to make them. Twenty witnesses had given statements to the prosecutors, al-Ahram said, in addition to electronic evidence that included conversations and video clips. According to the state-run Akhbar al-Youm newspaper, when asked by the judge about her alleged role during a court appearance last September, Khalifa said she had never seen any drugs until she was photographed with them inside the anti-narcotics authority offices. According to a 2025 Amnesty International report, there were 492 death sentences in the course of the year, 23 of whom were executed. The defendants were found guilty of drug trafficking and rape, "crimes that did not amount to 'intentional killing' to which the use of the death penalty must be restricted under international law and standards", the report said.
entry.summary: TV presenter among 11 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case BBC Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime The Guardian Egypt sentences TV host to death by hanging over drug trafficking Ynetnews Mission Impossible presenter sentenced to death in drugs case ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation Egyptian TV Presenter Sentenced to Death in Massive Drug Case Yahoo

entry.title: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway - BBC
entry.body: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway The Prince of Wales will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, Buckingham Palace has announced. Also going to the funeral, in a personal capacity, is Princess Anne, who is godmother to Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII. The late King Harald, a popular, modernising figure who had been on the Norwegian throne for 35 years, died last month at the age of 89. Royal sources say Prince William's attendance, representing his father King Charles, follows the convention that the monarch does not usually go to the funeral of another head of state. Large crowds are expected for the farewell to King Harald on 9 September, with a funeral procession to be followed by a service at Oslo Cathedral. Thousands have queued to pay their respects to the late king, during his lying in state in the chapel of the Royal Palace in the Norwegian capital. At the funeral, alongside Prince William, will be the widowed Queen Sonja, members of the Norwegian royal family including new King Haakon VIII, and other European royals. The service will be followed by a private burial in Norway's royal mausoleum in the Akershus Fortress. Among the tributes to King Harald was an emotional televised speech by his son King Haakon, who said: "Thank you for being such a good dad." Harald had been seen as a down to earth "people's king" who had helped to modernise the monarchy, broken with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure. His son said he represented the values of a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value". King Charles's message praised his cousin King Harald for serving his people with "unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility". King Haakon assumes his role at a difficult time, with the Norwegian royal family facing scandals this year. His wife, Queen Mette-Marit, came under scrutiny when it was revealed she had maintained a three-year friendship with the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised. Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. While Prince William will be in Norway, King Charles has returned to Scotland, after meeting President Macron of France at the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London this week. The King will be hosting Andy Burnham at Balmoral this weekend, in the traditional annual visit of the prime minister to stay with the monarch.
entry.summary: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway BBC Prince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway’s King Harald V The Guardian Princess Astrid of Norway alone with her brother's coffin: The last of her generation says goodbye to King Harald HOLA What the Death of Norway’s King Harald Teaches Us About Christ the King National Catholic Register Prince William and Princess Royal to attend King Harald’s funeral The Telegraph

entry.title: 'Can't Message That Away': GOP Frets as Trump Administration Desperately Spins Record-High Diesel Prices - Common Dreams
entry.body: But President Trump has pushed American energy dominance, we are producing more energy now than in the past." Duffy added that "it's only President Trump who's trying to drive these prices down," even though the president's war has been the primary reason they've been going up. Fox & Friends weekend host Charlie Hurt gives Trump credit for record high diesel prices: "Uhhh, they'd be a lot higher if it wasn't for the efforts of the administration" "When you look at diesel, you have to look at Russia and Ukraine," Duffy replies 🥴 pic.twitter.com/Wm5bLJ6exA — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) September 5, 2026 As a report published Friday by The Associated Press explained, the cost of diesel has a particularly strong impact on the price of food since the fuel is used to power both farm equipment and the trucks used to deliver food to grocery stores. "Fuel accounts for roughly 15% to 30% of the total cost of food, according to the Independent Grocers Alliance, a grouping of 7,500 global supermarkets," reported the AP. "So higher diesel costs often result in more expensive groceries, although it can take a while for energy shocks to wind their way through the supply chain." The rising cost of groceries has been a major source of stress for US consumers for years, and Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign vowed that prices on groceries would come down starting on his very first day in office.

entry.title: Ganymede may hold more liquid water than all of Earth’s oceans combined, yet this immense reservoir is buried beneath roughly 150 kilometres of ice—and scientists still do not know whether any of it has ever reached the surface. - spacedaily.com
entry.body: Ganymede may contain more liquid water than all of Earth’s surface oceans combined. The scale is difficult to reconcile with the moon’s dry, battered appearance. There are no open seas, no dark fractures spilling water vapour and no confirmed plume delivering a sample into space. The reservoir inferred inside Jupiter’s largest moon is hidden beneath an icy shell that a widely cited model places at roughly 150 kilometres thick. The ocean itself may be about 100 kilometres deep. Wrapped around a world larger than Mercury, even an uncertain liquid layer of those dimensions becomes immense. Yet neither number came from a drill, a radar profile reaching the ocean or a spacecraft floating above liquid water. Scientists inferred the sea through Ganymede’s magnetic behaviour and the motion of its auroras, then used interior models to estimate where the liquid could reside. The surface complicates the story. Ancient grooves and smoother terrain have been interpreted as signs of internal activity. Juno detected salts and organic compounds that could be remnants of subsurface brine. But no observation has demonstrated a continuous route from the present deep ocean to the exterior. That distinction separates Ganymede from Enceladus, where an ocean advertises itself through geysers. Ganymede may possess the larger reservoir while keeping it behind a far more effective wall. “More water than Earth” is a modelled volume Ganymede’s mean radius is about 2,631 kilometres, making it the largest moon in the Solar System and slightly wider than Mercury. Its density is much lower than Mercury’s because a substantial part of Ganymede consists of water ice rather than metal and rock. SpaceDaily previously examined why Ganymede behaves like a full-sized world despite orbiting as a moon. Its iron-rich core, rocky mantle, intrinsic magnetic field and thick outer water layer mark a body that separated into distinct internal regions early in its history. NASA’s account of the Hubble aurora investigation gives the numbers most often repeated: an ocean estimated to be about 100 kilometres thick beneath a crust of mostly ice roughly 150 kilometres deep. NASA says that ocean is thought to contain more water than all the water on Earth’s surface. The comparison normally means Earth’s oceans and other surface water, not every water molecule locked in Earth’s mantle. It also does not mean all of Ganymede’s water is liquid. Ice may account for much of the moon’s enormous water inventory, and the fraction that is ocean depends on pressure, temperature, salinity and the thermal history assumed by a model. Because Ganymede is so large, even a global liquid shell tens of kilometres deep represents a tremendous volume. The broad conclusion does not require every published interior model to agree. The precise headline number does. The first convincing evidence came from magnetism A buried ocean cannot reflect sunlight toward a camera. Salt water can, however, conduct electricity. Put a conducting layer inside Jupiter’s changing magnetic environment and electrical currents develop within it. Those currents produce a secondary magnetic field that can be detected from outside the moon. Galileo’s magnetometer found evidence for such an induced response during close encounters with Ganymede. The interpretation is not perfectly simple because Ganymede also generates its own permanent magnetic field, the only moon known to do so. Researchers must separate the core-driven field, Jupiter’s field, magnetospheric plasma and the weaker response induced in the suspected ocean. Hubble supplied a different magnetic probe in 2015. Ganymede has faint auroral bands near its poles. As Jupiter’s field changes around the moon, those ovals should rock back and forth by about six degrees if no conducting ocean intervenes. Hubble observations found movement of only about two degrees. A salty ocean provides the leading explanation. Its induced magnetic field opposes part of Jupiter’s varying influence, damping the auroral motion. The result strengthened the ocean case without revealing the liquid directly. This kind of indirect evidence is why the list of ocean worlds has expanded so rapidly. As SpaceDaily reported in its survey of six moons with hidden seas, gravity, libration, magnetism and heat can expose liquid water even when the surface remains frozen. The 150-kilometre shell is not a measured wall It is useful to picture 150 kilometres of ice, but misleading to treat the figure as a known, uniform thickness. The magnetic observations constrain combinations of ocean depth, conductivity and thickness. Different assumptions about dissolved salts and internal temperature can produce different structures that fit portions of the data. Juno added a more direct thermal constraint during its June 2021 flyby. The spacecraft’s microwave radiometer sampled radiation emerging from different depths beneath the surface. A 2023 analysis of those measurements placed an upper bound of about 150 kilometres on the conducting part of the ice shell in the region observed. More recent reviews commonly describe a range around 80 to 150 kilometres. That still does not amount to a radar track reaching a sharp ice-water boundary. Microwave brightness depends on temperature, density, porosity, purity and liquid content. The Juno result is valuable because it narrows a model, not because it has supplied a photograph of the ocean roof. There may not be one simple roof. At the pressures inside a large icy moon, water freezes into dense crystalline forms unlike ordinary surface ice. Some models place the liquid between ordinary ice above and high-pressure ice below. Others permit several liquid and solid layers, the “club sandwich” structure used in many descriptions of Ganymede. The deepest liquid may therefore be separated from the rocky mantle by high-pressure ice. On Earth, the seafloor supplies minerals and chemical gradients that support ecosystems independent of sunlight. If Ganymede’s water cannot readily touch silicate rock, one potentially useful source of nutrients and energy becomes less accessible. Water vapour above Ganymede is not ocean spray Hubble observations announced in 2021 found the first evidence of water vapour in Ganymede’s tenuous atmosphere. The discovery sounds like a possible leak until its geography is considered. The vapour appeared where surface temperatures around local noon can become warm enough for exposed ice to sublimate, changing directly from solid to gas. NASA’s analysis of the water-vapour signal therefore attributed it to surface frost, not to an Enceladus-like plume rising from the global ocean. At Enceladus, Cassini flew through material expelled from an ocean-connected plume and measured water, salts, organics, molecular hydrogen and phosphorus. SpaceDaily’s account of sampling Enceladus without drilling through its ice shows the enormous scientific advantage of a sea that sends material into space. Ganymede offers no confirmed equivalent. Its thin exosphere proves that water molecules can leave the surface. It does not show that deep ocean water completed the journey. Salts on the surface are the strongest clue to exchange The surface itself contains more suggestive evidence. Ganymede has old, dark, cratered terrain and somewhat younger bright terrain scored by grooves, ridges and faults. Early interpretations proposed that watery or slushy eruptions resurfaced some regions. Later high-resolution Galileo images showed that tectonic stretching and deformation could explain much of the bright ground, leaving unequivocal cryovolcanic deposits rare at best. Juno’s infrared spectrometer changed the chemical side of the argument. During the 2021 close pass, it mapped parts of the Jupiter-facing hemisphere at better than one kilometre per pixel. Researchers reported hydrated sodium chloride, ammonium chloride, carbonates and possible organic compounds. The 2023 Nature Astronomy study found the materials concentrated in regions partly protected from Jupiter’s most destructive charged particles by Ganymede’s own magnetic field. The authors interpreted their composition and distribution as evidence for the extrusion of subsurface brines whose chemistry may reflect water-rock interaction inside the moon. That is meaningful evidence, but the word “subsurface” covers an enormous vertical range. A brine could have occupied shallow pockets created by local melting. It could have migrated upward in stages. It could record an ancient period when the ice shell was thinner and warmer. Salts left on the surface do not preserve a labelled depth of origin. This is why two apparently contradictory statements can both be responsible. Researchers can say that the salts suggest remnants of deep brine reached the surface, while planetary-protection assessments say there are no demonstrated indications that Ganymede’s present deep ocean is in contact with the exterior. Could the deep ocean ever cross that much ice? A thick shell does not make exchange physically impossible. It changes the mechanisms and timescales available. Large impacts can excavate material from depth, although piercing a 100-kilometre barrier requires conditions very different from opening a shallow crack. Warm ice can rise slowly, carrying chemical traces from an ocean interface toward shallower layers without transporting liquid all the way. Tectonic extension can thin and fracture the shell. Thermal plumes can create pockets of melt. In Ganymede’s past, a more eccentric orbit and stronger tidal heating may have made these processes substantially more effective than they are now. A 2025 review of exchange on the Jovian moons concluded that Ganymede may have experienced indirect transport and impact-driven exchange more than a billion years ago. It also emphasised the limitations of the present evidence. The likely age of the relevant terrain makes an ancient connection easier to defend than an active one. ESA’s current JUICE planetary-protection explanation is unusually blunt: as things stand, there are no indications that Ganymede’s deep subsurface ocean can be in contact with the icy surface. That conclusion governs contamination rules, but it is not a declaration that exchange never happened. It describes what has been demonstrated well enough for present mission planning. JUICE can narrow the gap without touching water ESA launched the Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, or JUICE, in April 2023. It is scheduled to reach Jupiter in July 2031 and, after a long tour of the system, enter orbit around Ganymede late in 2034. No spacecraft has previously orbited a moon beyond Earth’s. The mission will still not drill 150 kilometres. Its value comes from combining measurements that respond to different parts of the same hidden structure. The magnetometer will measure Ganymede’s intrinsic and induced fields over many geometries. Radio science will map gravity and its tidal variation. Laser altimetry will measure how the surface flexes. Ice-penetrating radar will search the upper crust for layering and pockets of liquid; only if the shell proves unexpectedly favourable could it approach the ocean interface. JUICE will also map surface composition and geology at far higher coverage than the scattered flybys available today. The mission’s Ganymede programme is designed to ask whether surface materials record tectonics, cryovolcanism, radiation processing or transport from deeper layers. The answer may be less dramatic than an erupting sea. It may show that ocean material rises only indirectly, over geological timescales, or that the modern reservoir is chemically isolated beneath multiple kinds of ice. Either result would change how scientists evaluate the moon as a possible habitat. For now, Ganymede presents a revealing mismatch. The evidence for an ocean is strong, and the likely water volume is vast. The evidence that this water has reached the surface is suggestive but unresolved. The largest hidden sea in the Solar System may also be one of the best sealed.
entry.summary: Ganymede may hold more liquid water than all of Earth’s oceans combined, yet this immense reservoir is buried beneath roughly 150 kilometres of ice—and scientists still do not know whether any of it has ever reached the surface. spacedaily.com

entry.title: Explore the globe in field recordings
entry.body: I love them when they’re incorporated into my ambient music. They’re great background noise for working or sleeping. But they’re also great for active listening, focusing in on the fine nuances of burbling brooks or urban chaos. Earth Garden gives you a globe to explore with real field recordings taken from various locations. Earth Garden is inspired by Radio Garden (which you should also check out) except, instead of exploring the world via radio, it’s environmental sounds. There are waves lapping at the shores of remote islands in the Atlantic, a chorus of crickets in Tanzania, and rainfall on the streets of Manhattan. (There’s a lot of rainfall, actually.) Explore the globe in field recordings Earth Garden takes you around the world using environmental audio from Freesound. The recordings are all pulled from Freesound, which does mean quality can vary, and volume between clips can be inconsistent. It also means that recordings tend to be more concentrated in the US and Europe, especially the UK. But it’s still quite fun and soothing to set the globe to rotate automatically, and as the reticle nears points on the Earth, it transitions to those new sounds. You can even click a button to put some generic ambient drones in the background. entry.title: Clucky’s new alarm app wakes you up with a crowing rooster
entry.body: I was yelled at by a rooster this morning. And no, I don’t live on a farm. The culprit was a newly launched iPhone app I downloaded. Meet Clucky, a new alarm app for habitual snoozers that gives you the option of being woken up by a rooster and then requires you to complete a mission before you can turn the alarm off. Clucky joins a growing category of alarm apps, including Alarmy and Awake, that use challenges to keep people from simply turning off their alarms and going back to sleep. Its funniest selling point is arguably the rooster option, but the app’s broader strategy is to make dismissing an alarm just irritating and ridiculous enough that users have no choice but to fully wake up. For those who prefer something a little more conventional, though, it also offers options like gentle chimes, peaceful birds, and the classic digital beeping noise. There’s also an “Extra Loud Mode” that cranks up the volume as soon as the alarm goes off. Clucky’s wake-up missions include solving math problems, memorizing and tapping tiles in the correct order, typing what Clucky says, shaking your phone, walking, doing push-ups, tilting a ball toward a goal, and completing an AI camera challenge. Additionally, there’s a detailed stats section that tracks the average number of seconds your alarm rings before you complete a mission, how many missions you’ve beaten, and your total number of wake-ups. You also get what the app calls a “Rooster Report,” which grades your wake-up performance for the week. Another neat feature is the ability to create a “Nest” or “Flock” with friends or family. These private alarm groups let people wake up at the same time and keep each other accountable. Clucky was founded by Adrian Angelo Abelarde, a former software engineer at Fanatics. Abelarde did not immediately respond to our request for comment. The app is currently available to download on the App Store. There’s a pro subscription priced at $39.99 per year.
entry.summary: Clucky's new alarm app has an option where users are woken up to the sound of a rooster. They then complete a mission to turn it off.

entry.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Passes 1 Million Copies Sold in Just 2 Days - IGN
entry.body: Single-player RPG and new IP The Blood of Dawnwalker has sold 1 million copies just two days after its launch, publisher Bandai Namco and developer Rebel Wolves have announced. Official social media accounts for the first-time developer's new game confirmed the news with a celebratory graphic today. The milestone was reached just 48 hours after The Blood of Dawnwalker launched for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S September 3. "Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community!" Rebel Wolves said in a message to fans. Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community! ❤ pic.twitter.com/9fNqO8gNGB — Dawnwalker (@DawnwalkerGame) September 5, 2026 An official summary for The Blood of Dawnwalker describes it as an "open-world dark fantasy action RPG set in 14th-century Europe." In this first chapter, players take the role of Coen, a "human by day and vampire by night" who is fighting for his family in a narrative shaped by player choice. It also happens to have an in-game clock that sees Coen's story take place through a 30-day period. It's something some players love – and others don't. Reaching 1 million copies sold in such a short amount of time would be an impressive feat for any game, but there are a few reasons it's especially noteworthy for the Rebel Wolves team. This is the studio's first major release since it was founded in 2022. Led by The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt director and Cyberpunk 2077 co-director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, The Blood of Dawnwalker is also a new IP. The Warsaw-based studio previously released a CGI teaser to tease how sequels could potentially expand on its dark fantasy formula in new and interesting ways. "The CGI teaser shows where the dark fantasy saga is heading," Bandai Namco said in a June press release. "Players can see Coen in completely different surroundings than the ones they are used to – a modern, 21st-century setting, offering a glimpse of where the overarching plot ultimately leads. As the developers revealed, the next installments of the Dawnwalker franchise will span centuries, continents, and cultures across the globe." Surreal. Thank you so much!🔥🙏 https://t.co/qhrBwsfOlv — Mateusz Tomaszkiewicz 🧛♂️ (@MTomaszkiewicz) September 5, 2026 Speechless. Tearing up a little 🥹 We're a passionate bunch. And we're not stopping here 😤 Thank you for trusting us ❤️ https://t.co/FCRMmJCBbP Tomaszkiewicz said at the time that each installment in the Dawnwalker series is planned to be a standalone entry "with its own story, without narrative cliffhangers, unresolved plot threads, or time travel ideas." With 1 million copies in players' hands out of the gate, those sequels already feel more likely to materialize. Although the when and where for these planned follow-ups have yet to be revealed, narrative director Jakub Szamałek has at least told fans to keep an eye out for "breadcrumbs related to the overarching plot spanning the saga" in The Blood of Dawnwalker. It helps that Rebel Wolves secured solid reviews upon the launch of its first game. IGN, for example, called it "amazing" in our 9/10 review. We said, "The Blood of Dawnwalker is an impressive, bloody cocktail of interesting ideas and well-written characters, making it one of this year’s best open-world RPGs." We'll have to wait to see what updates Bandai Namco and Rebel Wolves have in store. In the meantime, you can read what Tomaszkiewicz had to tell us when it comes to the studio's plans to establish even more new IP. For everything you need to know before starting the game yourself, click here. Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

entry.title: CD sales are booming as physical media continues its resurgence
entry.body: According to the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), CD sales exploded in the first half of 2026. A new report from the organization says 17.5 million CDs were sold in the first six months of the year, up from just 12 million during the same period in 2025. That’s a jump of 45.7 percent, and 58.6 percent in dollars, which reached $171.1 million. What makes this all the more shocking is that CD sales actually shrank 22 percent from 2024 to 2025. CD sales are booming as physical media continues its resurgence But don’t think that means people are abandoning streaming. The RIAA isn’t the only one to notice the boom in CD sales. In July, research firm Luminate released a report saying that 16.3 million units were sold in the first half of 2026. It suggested that much of that increase was due to special editions from K-Pop acts like BTS and that Gen Z and millennials were treating them mostly as collectibles, saying that only about half of buyers actually owned a CD player. Vinyl continued its resurgence as well, with the number of units sold climbing by nearly 21 percent from last year to 26.5 million. “Other physical” media, which includes CD singles, DVDs, cassettes, SACD, DVD-Audio… basically anything besides “standard vinyl and CD albums,” also surged by over 73 percent, to 1.6 million units. Despite the increased interest in physical media and the ongoing iPod revival, people are not leaving streaming in droves. Streaming revenue grew by 4.7 percent to $4.9 billion — dwarfing all physical media combined.

entry.title: Michigan football stuns WMU with miracle Hail Mary after game seemed over - Detroit Free Press
entry.body: Michigan football stuns WMU with miracle Hail Mary after game seemed over Appalachian State, Toledo and now Western Michigan — or, er, not. The Kyle Whittingham era of Michigan football looked like it had fizzled in spectacular fashion for the better part of 60 minutes against Western Michigan, as the No. 16 Wolverines scored on their opening drive then didn’t score again ... until after the clock hit zero. The game appeared over on Saturday, Sept. 5, when a Hail Mary attempt by Bryce Underwood from the Block "M" at midfield with 9 seconds left went out the back of the end zone as time expired. Western Michigan players rushed the field at Michigan Stadium, celebrating just the second victory by a Mid-American Conference team over U-M, and the first since 2008. But a replay review placed 1 second back on the clock, giving Michigan new life. And Underwood connected with receiver JJ Buchanon, himself a transfer from Utah, where he played for Whittingham, for the winning score and a surreal finish with a 13-12 score: Thousands of Michigan fans rushing the Big House turf to celebrate a victory over WMU. The game appeared to flip late in the first half. U-M led 7-3 and got the ball with less than a minute to play. Rather than take a knee, U-M attempted to extend its lead, with Underwood throwing a careless interception — on a 5-yard out-route deep in U-M territory with 12 seconds left — that was returned for a touchdown, before officials ruled Dillon Moore stepped out of bounds on his return. The defense, which held strong for the most part and didn’t allow a touchdown, did allow the Broncos to go on a 20-play, 71-yard drive that melted 13:40 off the clock and gave WMU a 9-7 lead with 10:25 to play. Michigan's next-to-last drive appeared to be the finale, as the Wolverines got the ball with 3:12 to play on their own 7. After Jordan Marshall picked up a 15-yard gain, Underwood appeared to have run for another, but the ball was punched out by Western’s Josh Franklin and recovered by Kedrick Burley at the U-M 31. Western picked up two first downs on the ground and kicked a field goal with 35 seconds left. Then it wasn’t Western Michigan outrushed U-M (132-106), ran more plays (67-48) had fewer penalties (Michigan had nine for 80 yards, WMU had five for 40 yards), fewer turnovers (3-0) and dominated time of possession (40:08-19:52). And yet, at the end, it was the maize and blue celebrating at Michigan Stadium. [ Make "Hail Yes!" your go-to weekly Wolverines podcast, available anywhere you listen to podcasts (Apple, Spotify) or watch live on YouTube. ] It was over when ... well, it wasn't It appeared to be after Underwood’s fumble, Western Michigan had to pick up one first down to truly put the game on ice. On the first snap, Jalen Buckley picked up 11 yards. U-M finally got a stop on the next set of downs and forced a WMU field goal to get the ball back on its 7 with 35 seconds left, down 12-7. It seemingly would take a miracle to go 93 yards in that time. Player of the game: Dom Nichols Teammate Blake Frazier said Nichols was “going to terrorize people” this season from the edge and that’s exactly what he did Saturday. Late in the first quarter, he sacked QB Broc Lowry on third down to force a punt. Two drives later, on second-and-1 in U-M territory, he sacked Lowry again on a speed-to-power rush to force third-and-long and an eventual punt. On the next drive, he beat a pulling guard on third-and-15 and dropped Jalen Buckley for a loss to knock the Broncos out of field goal range. The junior was everywhere for the Wolverines, finishing with nine tackles, including 2½ for loss — perhaps the bright spot of the evening until the final moment of the game. Trending up: JJ Buchanan While the offense didn’t impress, transfer wide receiver JJ Buchanan did, even before his winning TD. He caught the opening pass for a gain of 8 on a slant, then hauled in a one-handed snag on a botched play moments later to pick up 20. In all he had more than half of U-M’s passing production, at least before he added to his total with the final Hail Mary catch. Trending down: Clean games Whittingham is known for teams that play disciplined football, but this maize-and-blue squad wasn’t that. Returner Andrew Marsh muffed a punt. Underwood threw an inexcusable pick and could’ve had three in the first half (one was dropped, another was touched by a defender with his toe on the sideline). Then, there were penalties – including too many illegal formation calls. Michigan also had two holding calls on the first drive of the second half that ended in a punt, then on the final play of the drive had 12 players on the field. Michigan football schedule: Oklahoma up next Week 2 brings a rematch with No. 9 Oklahoma (1-0), which rolled over Michigan last season in Norman, Oklahoma. This game, however, will be in Ann Arbor – just the third visit to Michigan from an SEC team this century – next Saturday (noon, Fox). The Sooners spent their Friday night in Week 1 showing why quarterback John Mateer – in his second season in Norman after transferring from Washington State – is a sleeper Heisman Trophy candidate. Mateer completed 11 of 17 passes for 225 yards and three TDs in limited action in a 51-0 victory over UTEP (Michigan’s Week 3 opponent). - Week 2: vs Oklahoma, Saturday, Sept. - Week 3: vs UTEP, Saturday, Sept. - Week 4: vs Iowa, Saturday, Sept. 26 (time and TV TBA). - Week 5: at Minnesota, Saturday, Oct. 3 (time and TV TBA). - Week 6: Bye week. - Week 7: vs Penn State, Saturday, Oct. 17 (time and TV TBA). - Week 8: vs Indiana, Saturday, Oct. 24 (time and TV TBA). - Week 9: at Rutgers, Saturday, Oct. 31 (time and TV TBA). - Week 10: vs Michigan State, Saturday, Nov. 7 (time and TV TBA). - Week 11: at Oregon, Saturday, Nov. 14 (time and TV TBA). - Week 12: vs UCLA, Saturday, Nov. 21 (time and TV TBA). - Week 13: at Ohio State, Saturday, Nov. Tony Garcia is the Michigan beat writer for the Detroit Free Press. Email him at apgarcia@freepress.com and follow him on X at @RealTonyGarcia. If you purchase through our links, the USA Today Network may earn a commission. Prices were accurate at the time of publication but may change.

entry.title: 'One of the best' - boxing world reacts to Taylor's farewell win - BBC
entry.body: 'One of the best' - boxing world reacts to Taylor's farewell win - Published Some of the biggest names in women's boxing have paid tribute to Katie Taylor after the Irish great ended her career with victory over Flora Pili at Croke Park. Unified lightweight champion Caroline Dubois called Taylor "one of the best to ever do it", while Claressa Shields said the 40-year-old deserved to "ride off into the sunset". Taylor beat Pili on points in Dublin to become undisputed light-welterweight champion and retires with 26 wins from 27 professional contests, Olympic gold and three undisputed title triumphs across two divisions. "Thank you so much for paving the way," Londoner Dubois wrote on X. "Wishing you happiness, success and joy for this next season." Taylor was sharper throughout, repeatedly beating the Frenchwoman to the punch before finishing with one final burst of combinations as the crowd rose to its feet. American Shields - the self-proclaimed Greatest Woman of All Time - added: "Congrats Katie. Now ride off into the sunset. You deserve it all." Super-featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner described Taylor as "a trailblazer who helped set the stage for all of us". "What a legacy," she wrote. "It's been a privilege watching your journey from the beginning." 'There will never be another one like her' Taylor's farewell unfolded in front of more than 80,000 fans in Dublin, with Westlife performing before the main event and Croke Park providing a fitting backdrop to her final night. Former world champion Carl Frampton said Taylor's relationship with the Irish public was unlike anything else in boxing. "You can tell that she doesn't enjoy doing stuff in front of the media, but she still has this adulation from everybody," the Northern Irishman said. "Katie Taylor is different, she's special and there will never be another one like her." Former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew described the occasion as one of the most remarkable exits the sport had seen. "I don't think in all of my years of watching this game, I have seen an exit as beautiful, amazing and fitting," he said. "She has just retired as the greatest champion ever. I have never seen a fighter leave as an undisputed champion on their own terms." Former world champion Barry Jones picked out the final 20 seconds, when Taylor produced the kind of rapid combinations which defined so many of her biggest fights. "That's what you really remember about her," he said on the Dazn broadcast. "Those rallies of big punches, combinations and that's how she finished her last fight." American Mikaela Mayer - who was also ringside - was struck by the final image of Taylor placing her gloves in the centre of the ring. "I was sitting there watching her put her gloves in the centre of the ring and it's like a story," she said. Taylor had long dreamed of fighting at Croke Park and had made clear she wanted the stadium to stage the final chapter of her career. Bellew said there was "no way" Taylor would return to boxing, although he could see her remaining involved by mentoring younger fighters. "She will always be there to give her advice, speak to her and help her," he said. "But ultimately she will sail off into the sunset and who could possibly deserve it more." entry.title: Gauff wins but mixed fortunes for home hopes at US Open
entry.body: Gauff wins but mixed fortunes for home hopes at US Open - Published Coco Gauff marched into the fourth round of the US Open but compatriots Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys exited on a mixed day for home hopes in New York. Gauff, the most recent American champion in New York in 2023, did not have things all her own way but maintained her bid for a second triumph by overcoming Spain's Cristina Bucsa 6-3 6-4. However, Keys said she felt "scared" as she slumped to defeat despite leading her third set against China's Zheng Qinwen 5-0, while last year's runner-up Anisimova lost in straight sets. There could yet be as many as five American women in the last 16, with Iva Jovic hoping to join Gauff, Jessica Pegula, Taylor Townsend and Emma Navarro in the fourth round. American players could also contest six of the eight fourth-round matches in the men's draw, with Ben Shelton, Frances Tiafoe, Tommy Paul and Alex Michelsen through - and Learner Tien and Michael Zheng still to play. - Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory - Published3 hours ago - Fritz and Cobolli shocked as men's seeds tumble - Published2 hours ago Gauff 'enjoying the experience' despite expectation Despite the weight of expectation that she has had to deal with from a young age at her home major, the 22-year-old Gauff is through to the second week at the US Open for a fifth successive year. Gauff, who became the first American teenager to win the US Open since Serena Williams in 1999 with her breakthrough major success three years ago, heads into the fourth round as the form player in the women's game. Victory over Bucsa was the 2025 French Open winner's eighth straight-set WTA Tour-level win in a row. The fourth round is where Gauff's US Open challenge ended in the previous two editions, and she admitted that she struggled to handle the pressure last year. But in recovering from a 3-1 deficit in the first set, and producing an immediate response to being broken to love in the second, Gauff demonstrated she is better placed to cope with that this time. "I feel like I'm used to getting to the second week now. I woke up today and I was like 'oh we're already in round three'," Gauff said. "There's expectations, being American, and I want to do well in front of the fans. "Last year, I put so much pressure on myself. I'm enjoying the experience out here." I got really scared - Keys Keys appeared on course for a first fourth-round appearance at her home slam since 2023 after taking a commanding third set lead against Olympic champion Zheng. But the 2025 Australian Open winner would miss a match point and lose each of the final seven games in a 1-6 7-6 (7-3) 7-5 loss that stunned the crowd. The 31-year-old Keys said she felt as though she "couldn't play tennis anymore" in the final set. "I obviously got off to a really good lead, and then I got really scared, like I couldn't swing [the racquet]," Keys said. "I felt like I couldn't play tennis anymore. It just felt like it was a much bigger deal than just playing a tennis match all of a sudden." Keys, who lost the 2017 US Open final to fellow American Sloane Stephens, went out in the fourth round at the other three majors in 2026. "I feel like I've been struggling for a while now. I'm going to have to make some sort of changes," Keys said. "I just kind of keep putting it off because that's how the tennis world works. It's just to the point where I actually need to do something about it." Anisimova, beaten by world number one Aryna Sabalenka in last year's US Open final, lost in straight sets to Russian-born Austrian 24th seed Anastasia Potapova. The 25-year-old was visibly frustrated with herself throughout the contest, losing her serve twice in the first set and four times in a topsy-turvy second. Related topics - Published28 August
entry.summary: Coco Gauff reaches the US Open fourth round but last year's finalist Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys go out on a mixed day for home hopes.

entry.title: Leistikow's 4 thoughts after Iowa football steamrolls NIU, 40-0 - Hawk Central
entry.body: Leistikow's 4 thoughts after Iowa football steamrolls NIU, 40-0 IOWA CITY — The ongoing quarterback discussion took a back seat, for a change, to other catalysts on offense in Iowa football’s season opener at Kinnick Stadium. And hello again, Kamari Moulton. 28 (Moulton) headlined the Hawkeyes’ early offensive fireworks in what evolved into a 40-0 rout of the helpless Huskies before 69,250 sweat-soaked fans on a sweltering afternoon. Iowa finished the game with 507 yards of offense, a new high for the three-year era of offensive coordinator Tim Lester and the most in a game for the Hawkeyes since gaining 644 in 2019 vs. Yes, it was Iowa's biggest offensive day in almost seven years. “We had a huge fall camp," Moulton said of the offense. "We were working very hard, and we wanted to prove that we could be a good team.” After one game, it’s too early to declare that Iowa has its best wide receiver since at least 2020. But the Hawkeyes featured Diaz from the get-go Sept. 5, like they know that they have something special in the Texas-Rio Grande Valley transfer. On Iowa’s first drive of the season, Diaz caught three passes for 32 yards — an early statement from Lester. Diaz also drew a pass-interference flag in the end zone to extend the drive, which he ended with a nifty 6-yard grab from Hank Brown in the back of the south end zone to score the Hawkeyes’ first touchdown of 2026. Diaz celebrated with thousands of new friends wearing gold in the stands. I needed it," Diaz said. For me, the first drive, I need a couple touches just to get out of my little shell. I mean, I was nervous all week.” Iowa passers targeted Diaz 13 times, a sign of how heavily he'll be involved in the game plan. By halftime, Diaz already had the most yards in a game by any Iowa wide receiver since Jacob Gill (138) on Nov. Iowa’s highest single-game total by a wide receiver over the last 16 games was Sam Phillips’ 75 yards vs. Diaz finished with seven receptions for 84 yards, and he made a catch of the day that didn’t count — hauling in a deflected pass in the end zone while lying on his back. Unfortunately, part of his body was out of bounds so it didn't count. Diaz also rushed once for 10 yards. Bottom line: Diaz looked like a difference-maker, backing up the hype he had been building since arriving in January. And his stats could’ve been better had Brown and Jeremy Hecklinski been more accurate. Hecklinski, in particular, had Diaz running behind the defense for what could’ve been a 38-yard touchdown in the third quarter but overthrew him on fourth-and-6. “There's always room for improvement," Diaz said. "We'll just get that down, watch film, and come back out here next week (Sept. Iowa State, 6:30 p.m., NBC) and put on another show.” After Diaz got things started, Moulton heated up behind a mauling performance from the interior of Iowa’s offensive line — Leighton Jones, Cael Winter and Kade Pieper. Moulton blasted into the end zone from 50 and 37 yards on back-to-back drives, and Iowa had a 20-0 lead with less than 11 minutes elapsed for the season. By halftime, Moulton had shattered his career high in rushing with 155 yards. It had been almost a cruel reality that he reached 90 yards five times last season but never got past 99. This was his second career 100-yard game, with a final total of 11 carries for 183 yards. Head coach Kirk Ferentz took time in his opening statement in his postgame news conference to praise the best game Moulton's had as a Hawkeye. "He just looked faster, quicker, more confident than I've seen him," Ferentz said. "He's an experienced football player, one of the guys we're definitely counting on. But I thought he really looked the best we've seen him." Moulton had been optimistic that he was set to take the next step as a running back this season, and he said finding confidence in his own ability was an offseason key. He's helped discover that with new running backs coach Jay Novell, and he sure looks better. And that’s a good thing because his presumed co-leader in the backfield, South Dakota transfer LJ Phillips, left the game in the first quarter with what appeared to be a left-ankle injury and didn’t return. Phillips finished with four carries for five yards. Iowa's running game mostly stalled without Moulton in there and Phillips sidelined, though Braden Jackson showed some flashes late off the bench. It's too early to say that's a concern, because offensive line coach George Barnett was shuttling in backups by the end of the first half, and second- and third-teamers played the second half (which saw no offensive touchdowns as Iowa took its foot off the gas). Hank Brown starts; how did the quarterbacks fare? Given what we saw on Kids Day at Kinnick three weeks earlier, a Brown start in the opener would have seemed very unlikely. Brown struggled in that open practice, and Hecklinski shined with a five-touchdown day. But credit to Brown, the Auburn transfer, for fighting back in the competition and ultimately earning the “first at-bat,” as Lester said, for the first game. And further credit to Brown, the offense functioned at a high level on those first three drives when he was at the helm. “I was able to have fun today and just grow in chemistry with my teammates," Brown said. Iowa scored touchdowns on drives of 75, 66 and 70 yards on a total of 16 Brown-led snaps before Hecklinski took the reins on drive No. Brown cooled off after that, misfiring on some throws, including what could’ve been a layup touchdown to DJ Vonnahme. Hecklinski, overall, was decent but inconsistent. For the day, I'd give Brown a B and Hecklinski a C-minus. “I was happy with the start," Brown said. "When I came back out there the second time, it was just (not) making the makeables. (I need) to make it easier on my guys, tight ends and receivers, just giving them a better opportunity, not making it a hard catch for them when they're open.” Their final numbers: Brown went 12-of-20 for 129 yards and one touchdown. Hecklisnki was 7-for-16 for 76 yards and one touchdown and one interception. Iowa scored 26 points on drives led by Brown and seven led by Hecklinski. They each had one nice run to gain a first down, and neither was sacked. Neither played in the fourth quarter as third-stringer Jimmy Sullivan took over for his first career snaps. He had played 12 total game snaps since the fall of 2023 as a high school senior in Marietta, Georgia. He played 31 on Saturday. “There was some nervousness going in at first. Obviously, haven't played in three years. Like this is Iowa, it’s a big program with 70,000 people here," Hecklinski said. "I just need to slow down on my reads. I was too quick on some things, and I gotta put some balls in better places.” Ferentz did not say how the quarterback situation would be handled going forward, but it's likely that they'll continue to rotate. That'd be good, because we didn't see either guy deliver an overwhelming performance. Iowa’s red-zone offense sorely missed Mark Gronowski, a touchdown machine inside the 5-yard line a year ago at quarterback. Iowa had a first-and-goal from NIU’s 1 in the third quarter and failed to score. Hecklinski threw incomplete across his body on an ill-advised throw. Then Hecklinski was intercepted on an end-zone attempt, Iowa’s first turnover of 2026. Hecklinski said the only reason he threw that ball was because it was fourth down, which was the right idea ... better to give it a chance than take a fourth-down sack. "Every week you have things to work on, but probably short-yardage and goal line would be at the top right now," Ferentz said. "You have to address that right away." A really encouraging day for Iowa’s defense Deshaun Lee officially got credit for Iowa’s first turnover on defense this season, but give the assist to the swarming mentality of Phil Parker’s defense. Northern Illinois opened its fourth possession at its own 34 early in the second quarter after Caden Buhr missed a 53-yard field goal. Quarterback Jalen Macon fled to his right, taking consistent hits and spinning until some combination of Zach Lutmer, Jayden Montgomery, Jacob Wallace and Drew Campbell got him (and his helmet) to the ground. Because the helmet came off, Macon had to leave for one play. That brought in Taron Dickens, the Western Carolina transfer, into the game. Dickens’ first pass at NIU was intercepted by Lee over the middle, and he returned the theft 17 yards into Huskies territory. A quick word about Lee after his fourth career interception: He was terrific, backing up Ferentz’s assertion that he was on a TJ Hall trajectory in his final year. Lee is off to a good start as Iowa’s No. “Anytime as a defensive back, you get your hands on the ball, that’s a great moment," Lee said. Iowa’s defense was as good as you could hope, holding Northern Illinois without a first down and only 23 yards on its first nine possessions. The Huskies' first first down of the game came with 4:10 left in the third quarter on an iffy pass-interference flag against Rashad Godfrey Jr. Northern Illinois didn't cross 100 yards for the game until the final 75 seconds. The Huskies were sacked six times and gained seven first downs. Of Iowa’s credited sacks, 1½ went to Joseph Anderson, one apiece to Chima Chineke and Julian Manson and a half-sack each to Bryce Hawthorne, Drew Campbell, Landyn Van Kekerix, Preston Ries and Khamari Brown. They helped record the 19th shutout of the 28-year Ferentz era. “Honestly it was the highlight of my day seeing those young guys get in there and making plays," Hawthorne said. "Like, how could it not put a smile on your face? That's what we want, and that's what we need to uphold, and that's what we did uphold.” A slow start, then a bang on special teams Walk-on Caden Buhr's first-ever extra-point attempt of college sailed wide right. It was an unfortunate start in his debut after winning the Hawkeyes' placekicker job over Eli Ozick. Buhr also missed his first field-goal attempt as a Hawkeye, though it was from 53 yards ... and he did have the distance but was wide right again. Buhr rallied to knock home field goals of 45 and 34 yards and the remainder of his PATs. Kick-coverage wise, Iowa was tremendous as always. True freshman Darion Jones delivered a wallop of a hit to get the day started on that front. Boston Everitt looked pretty good at punter (three boots for a 43.7-yard average) and was praised by Ferentz. And then at punt return? We surprisingly didn't see Zach Lutmer as the return man, as the nod instead went to Reece Vander Zee in the first half then Evan James in the second half. And with former special-teams coordinator LeVar Woods on hand (watching his son, Mason, after Woods and Michigan State knocked off Toledo, 30-20, on Friday night), James did Iowa special teams proud with an electric 77-yard punt-return touchdown to push Iowa's lead to 40-0 late in the third quarter. Overall, it was a solid start for new special-teams coordinator Chris Polizzi. The blocking on James' speedy punt return looked like what we have come to expect from Hawkeye special teams. Between offense, defense and special teams, it was a day Ferentz felt good about. "Pleased about the outcome and then certainly proud of the team," Ferentz said. "I think they really did a good job today. Certainly showed up and played hard and they competed. "The bigger picture: I thought they did a good job with the preparation all week, and that showed up today." Hawkeyes columnist Chad Leistikow has served for 31 years with The Des Moines Register and USA TODAY Sports Network. Chad is the 2023 INA Iowa Sports Columnist of the Year and NSMA Co-Sportswriter of the Year in Iowa. Join Chad's text-message group at HawkCentral.com/HawkeyesTexts.

entry.title: Oklahoma State football embarrassed by Tulsa to start Eric Morris era: Replay, highlights - The Oklahoman
entry.body: Oklahoma State football embarrassed by Tulsa to start Eric Morris era: Replay, highlights Tre Lamb was right. It was around seven months ago when Tulsa’s football coach declared to Golden Hurricane fans that his team would “beat their a-- again” during their rematch with Oklahoma State. It felt a tad foolish with the new regime taking over in Stillwater. In what could be described as a true failure, the Cowboys were a mess in Eric Morris’ head coaching debut, falling 24-10 at Tulsa on Saturday. It’s the second straight season the Golden Hurricane upset the Cowboys, who opened the week as a two-touchdown favorite. Instead, the Pokes were fortunate to get into the end zone just once. The new-look offense led by quarterback Drew Mestemaker stalled, particularly on fourth-down plays. OSU was 2 of 6 on that down. Mestemaker was 29 of 49 for 241 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions. Running back Caleb Hawkins rushed for 79 yards on 18 carries. OSU’s defense was mostly solid and kept the Cowboys in the game, though it wore down in the second half as Tulsa started to pull away. The Golden Hurricane totaled 363 yards. And after Tulsa’s Damari Alston scored his second TD on a 29-yard rush with 7:52 left for a 24-10 lead, it was all but over. Then it was basically sealed when Zach Williams intercepted Mestemaker in the end zone with 4:13 remaining. That leaves a really sour taste in the mouths of the Cowboys as they go to Week 2 with a matchup against College Football Playoff contender Oregon.
