entry.title: UFC Paris: Michael 'Venom' Page wins in underwhelming UFC farewell - BBC
entry.body: Fans boo as MVP wins in underwhelming UFC farewell - Published Michael 'Venom' Page's last fight on his UFC contract ended in an underwhelming win against Nursulton Ruziboev amid booing fans in Paris. London's Page, who is nicknamed 'MVP', landed a handful of eye-catching strikes during the contest but could not deliver the knockout that the fans craved as he won by unanimous decision. The 39-year-old's victory means all five of his wins in the UFC since joining in 2024 have come via decision. Page joined the UFC with a reputation as an innovative striker with a resume of highlight-reel knockouts, but admitted pre-fight he has underperformed since joining the organisation. Page said the fight with Uzbekistan's Ruziboev was "important to re-establish myself with the UFC", but he did not get the finish he wanted. Page, who arrived in the UFC over two years ago with 13 knockouts to his name, received a raucous ovation from the French crowd as he entered the octagon. Ruziboev controlled the majority of the first round on the ground before Page started to open up midway through the fight. He landed a kick to Ruziboev's knee which wobbled the 32-year-old, before smiling and showboating as he delivered a number of feints. Page delivered an overhead right and an elbow, but the explosive moments were few and far between as the crowd grew frustrated at a lack of action. Throughout the bout, Page landed only 12 significant strikes to Ruziboev's eight. Page has shown throughout his UFC career he is a master of movement and evasion, without having the finishing instinct that the most successful fighters possess. The fight against Ruziboev followed the same pattern, and although Page was awarded victory by the judges, his arm was raised after jeers from the crowd. With Page now a free agent, potential options for him if he does not re-sign with the UFC include joining the PFL or turning to boxing. In the main event, French-Moroccan Salahdine Parnasse earned a stunning first-round TKO win over Dan Hooker. Parnasse was making his UFC debut and delivered in front of a home crowd, landing a punishing kick to the body before dropping New Zealand's Hooker with a left hook. The 28-year-old followed with a flurry of punches as Hooker, ranked 12 in the lightweight division, shelled up on the floor, forcing the referee to wave off the contest. There was also victory for fellow Briton Kurtis Campbell, who submitted American Trevor Peek in the third round of their featherweight bout via a rear-naked choke. It was a return to winning ways for the 24-year-old Liverpudlian, who lost on his UFC debut to Danny Silva in March. Campbell's win extends his professional record to nine wins and one defeat. "I know my debut didn't go the way I wanted it to but I'm here to show I'm the real deal and the future is bright," said Campbell. Earlier on the card, London's Nathaniel Wood lost by unanimous decision to Moldova's Pavel Andrusca, bringing his four-fight win streak to an end. Andrusca, who was a late replacement after Wood's original opponent Mairon Santos withdrew 10 days prior to the fight, extended the unbeaten start to his career to nine. At UFC 322 on 3 October in Salt Lake City, it was announced Brazil's Natalia Silva will fight for the vacant flyweight title against China's Wang Cong. Former title holder Valentina Shevchenko has vacated the belt and is set to miss over a year with injury, according to the UFC. entry.title: Tears, blood & triumph - Taylor's iconic career in pictures
entry.body: Making her amateur debut in 2001, Taylor won every medal and title she could have and more importantly had a lasting effect on women's boxing and women as athletes. BBC Sport takes a look back on some of the best pictures from her iconic career. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Taylor helped legalise women boxing in Ireland, competing in the first sanctioned female fight in 2001 aged 15 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Taylor won five world championships as an amateur including in 2012 when she also won Olympic gold in London Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Her father Peter, who had been her long-time coach, was there to celebrate with her Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Taylor is one of 15 Irish athletes to win gold at an Olympics in any sport and was the only Irish gold medallist in 2012 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, She returned in 2016 but suffered a shock exit in the quarter-finals Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Taylor quickly moved on, convincing Matchroom promoter Eddie Hearn to sign her as a professional. Taylor was the first female fighter Hearn signed Image source, Getty Images Image caption, She made a winning debut at Wembley Arena in November 2016, which was packed with Irish fans Image source, Getty Images Image caption, She took just 11 months to claim her first world title - the WBA lightweight belt Image source, Getty Images Image caption, In her bid to become Ireland's first four-belt world champion at Madison Square Garden in 2019, she was almost beaten by Delfine Persoon Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The wounds of war were obvious on Taylor's face after the battle with Persoon Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Taylor returned to MSG in 2022, this time to face Amanda Serrano. Years of talks finally bore fruit as the rivals finally stepped in the ring together at a sold-out MSG. entry.title: Bad Bunny ‘Super Bowl Halftime Show,’ ‘Muppets’ and ‘Traitors’ Win Night 1 Creative Arts Emmy Awards
entry.body: Bad Bunny’s “Super Bowl Halftime Show” and “The Traitors” dominated night one of the Creative Arts Emmys with seven and six wins, respectively. Comedian Wanda Sykes provided opening remarks. “Television isn’t made by a handful of people. It’s made by thousands of talented people solving impossible problems together to create something great,” she said. “So, the more excellence there is to recognize, the more time we should spend celebrating it.” The first Emmy of the evening went to late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel, who won for game show host (“Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?”). Kimmel, who won last year, thanked the seat fillers. He joked, “Mostly I really want to thank whoever decided to put our category first because we won last year, and it was nothing but seat fillers. So, thank you very much, and thanks to the seat fillers for sticking it out.” “The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny” picked up seven Emmys, including outstanding choreography for variety or reality programming (Charm La’Donna, Karina Ortiz), outstanding production design for a variety special Bruce Rodgers), outstanding music direction (Miguel Gandelman) and outstanding variety special (live). Gandelman talked about the challenge of putting the show together. He said, “The hardest part for me was catching Benito on tour. I had to record the band, so I had to go to Colombia. I had to go to Chile.” He went on to say, “Production in L.A. had started already, so making sure that I was always on time with everything that was needed for me.” Mariska Hargitay took home two Emmys for outstanding documentary or nonfiction special and outstanding directing for “My Mom Jayne: A Film By Mariska Hargitay.” During her speech, an emotional Hargitay honored feminist icon Gloria Steinem, who died earlier this week. Hargitay said, “My hero and friend Gloria Steinem recently said, ‘Please tell your own story. The most important thing that we can do for each other is to know each other through stories.’” A tearful Hargitay said, “I got to know my mother through telling the story, and it is a gift that is indescribable.” Backstage, Hargitay talked further about Steinem and what her win meant to women. She said, “Don’t let anyone else define you. Dreaming, as Gloria said, is part of planning.” Hargitay said, “I’m at a place in my life where I just say yes. I said yes to Broadway, and I said yes to hosting the Emmys.” She went on to say, “When they called me, I thought it was a joke, and then I went, ‘Why not?” So, it’s a year of firsts and a year of saying yes and a year of not limiting myself or not being governed by fear.” She concluded by saying, “What if it all works out? That’s the process of art.” Sabrina Carpenter is now halfway to EGOT winning an Emmy in the outstanding variety special (pre-recorded) for “The Muppet Show.” Carpenter is created as an executive producer and performer for the series. Seth Rogen also took home his fifth Emmy award for his work as an executive producer. Tyler Strickland, who won the Emmy for outstanding music composition for a documentary/nonfiction or reality for “John Candy: I Like Me,” spoke backstage about his approach to scoring the film. Strickland said he recorded the entire score using a string orchestra. “For John specifically, with his theme, I gave him a French horn, which I think really spoke to valor and strength, but also was a singular instrument that I could write sad melodies on and try to give him a little bit of a synthesis.” Talking about his biggest challenge, he said, “We were making a film about somebody who’s so iconic and known for all these amazing roles, but that we weren’t making a comedic film. We were making a beautiful film about a father and a husband and a man who was struggling with anxiety.” Netflix’s “Love on a Spectrum” took home three Emmys. During his acceptance speech, casting director Sean Bowman, who won for outstanding casting for a reality program, said working on the show “is an absolute dream.” Bowman said, “I want to thank our casting team, Chelsea (Darnell, casting producer), and the cast who trusted us with their stories and the thousands of people who have written in.” Bowman went on to say, “I just love talking on Zoom and hearing their stories of why they want to find love. If you want to find love, you can find love.” Popular on Variety The previously announced juried awards were also handed out this evening. Adult Swim’s “Genndy Tartakovsky’s Primal” took home two Emmys for outstanding individual achievement in animation. Peacock’s “The Traitors” and Fox’s “The Masked Singer” were honored in the outstanding costumes for variety, nonfiction or reality programming categories. The Creative Arts Emmys are being handed out at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, and an edited presentation of the 2026 ceremonies will broadcast on Sept. 12, at 8:00 PM ET/PT on FXX. entry.title: ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore Is Astonishing in Jesse Eisenberg’s Funny and Dizzying Community-Theater Comedy
entry.body: It’s rare these days to find comedy and humanity on the same plate — and even more rare to see comedy nuzzling up to mystery. (I don’t mean mystery as in crime-solving; I mean the mystery of existence.) But Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” a small-town-theater comedy driven by big ideas, is a funny and dizzying mind-bender. It’s like “Waiting for Guffman” made by the Coen brothers at their most rivetingly unhinged. “The Debut” won’t be for everyone, but if you get onto its wavelength (which I did immediately), it sucks you into its “Twilight Zone of Sub-Broadway” vortex, even as the tone remains light and ticklish and surprising. Eisenberg, as he proved two years ago in the brilliant “A Real Pain,” is a grounded filmmaker (he loves reality). But here he’s working on a high wire of matter-of-fact satire that edges, just barely, into the surreal. At heart, the film is a twisted love letter to the glory of community theater. What holds it together is the suppleness of Eisenberg’s voice as a writer-director (the wit that singes, the story that never stops poking around corners), and the utterly astonishing performance of Julianne Moore, who plays a crumpled wallflower in dire need of blooming. Popular on Variety Moore’s Mona Friedman is a New Jersey homemaker who has become a Stepford zombie, because no one seems to need her anymore. Her twins, Matty (Joan Diamand) and Maya (Becca Suskauer), are nearly adults, and though they’re still living at home they’ve already checked out. Her husband, Howard (Patrick Fabian), is a handsome stiff-necked jerk who treats Mona like an accessory. And she’s such a fearful, passive people pleaser that none of this is in any danger of changing. Moore, with red eyes and translucent skin, gives off the aura of a damaged doll. In the opening scene, set in the Brook Theater, she tries out for a small role in the annual local production of “Nosy Neighbors,” and her audition is so weak that we don’t see how she could possibly get the part. It goes instead to Serena Cherry (Bernadette Peters), a Broadway wannabe who lands any role she wants. (There’s a poster of her in the lobby as the lead in a production of “Evita.”) But then, late one night, Mona gets a call from the musical’s director, Jerry (Paul Giamatti). Serena has bowed out; he’s got no one else to do the part. (It helps that she ripped off all the phone-number tags on a local flyer for the audition.) Mona comes into rehearsal the next morning (the cast has been at it for several weeks), and what we instantly see is that “Nosy Neighbors,” an upbeat musical about the residents of a downscale apartment building, is a corny but oddly sturdy piece of third-rate hokum – it’s like “Rent” redone by Corky St. (The songs, which Eisenberg composed, sound like Jonathan Larson-by-numbers.) Mona is playing Miss Danielle, the building super, a tough nut who wears a tool belt and has the signature line, “Rent’s due!” Not exactly an acting challenge. The other cast members are warm and welcoming, but Mona, who has no theatrical experience (beyond singing in her church choir until she was 13), is awful beyond words. She delivers that line as if she was whispering it in a library. She’s a doormat in life and a washout of an actress, even for community theater. So Jerry, realizing that he’s got a potential disaster on his hands, decides that his only recourse is to give Mona a tough-love private acting lesson. In a remarkable scene, he makes her ask for the rent check he’s holding in his hand — and more than that, he keeps asking her why she wants it, breaking down her defenses. It’s like a Sanford Meisner exercise turned torture session, and Mona finally busts through with a monologue that spills out of her guts, about how she wants that rent money because if she doesn’t get it she’ll be in an alley eating plague-ridden rats. She burns through her own lack of purpose and identity and, at that moment, becomes an actress. What Jerry doesn’t realize is that he’s created a monster. “The Debut” is at once an affectionate homage to the wide-eyed passion of community theater; a deftly original thriller; a parable of self-esteem; a teasing mockery of the mechanisms of self-esteem; and a one-woman psychodrama in which Mona discovers who she is by leaving her old reality behind. There’s a hilarious scene in which Jerry, as part of Mona’s Method training, takes her out to a random apartment building, and she talks her way into someone’s home by impersonating the super and demanding to fix the toilet. The thing is, the Method training works. Mona lets herself go and becomes a confident actress. Yet if that’s all there was to it, “The Debut” would just be a tidy feel-good fable. Eisenberg is too talented and ambitious to make that kind of movie. He wants instead to make our heads spin by taking us down a rabbit hole. It’s when Mona, fed up with her husband, moves out of her home and into a fleabag hotel, where the faucets drip and the dingy electric lights are buzzy and there are strange sounds coming through the walls, that the film begins to turn into a slightly dreamy hellscape. But Moore keeps us on her side. Her Mona is avid to find a new way to be, even if that means putting on a janitor suit and, after shorting out the hotel’s electricity (and burning off her eyebrows), getting a new look that makes her resemble Camille Paglia crossed with Joan Jett as styled by David Lynch. The joke, and it’s a juicy one, is that she has now gone full Method, and insists that everything her character in the musical says must be entirely reality-based. It wouldn’t work if Mona’s fearless new acting ethos weren’t so goddamn funny. And it wouldn’t work if Paul Giamatti, who’s kind of playing the audience’s surrogate, didn’t invest Jerry, the disgruntled theater romantic, with a hope and rage and bone-deep melancholy that keeps the film from flying off into the ether. The actors playing the song-and-dance cast members of “Nosy Neighbors” (they include Eisenberg) perform with sublimely subtle cluelessness. But it’s the audacity of Julianne Moore — now clenched, now grinning, now timid, now acting — that brings “The Debut” to its gratifying conclusion, as Mona, through the theater, discovers an extraordinary new role: herself.
entry.summary: What holds it together is the suppleness of Eisenberg’s voice as a writer-director (the wit that singes, the story that never stops poking around corners), and the utterly astonishing performance of Julianne Moore, who plays a crumpled-up wallflower in dire need of blooming. Oh, does she bloom.

entry.title: Danny Boyle Confirms Use Of AI In New Movie ‘Ink’ - Deadline
entry.body: Danny Boyle has confirmed the use of AI in new movie Ink about the launch of The Sun newspaper. Speaking to Vanity Fair, Boyle said he had used around 30 seconds of generative AI in the making of his new movie, which opened the Venice Film Festival this week before going on to play Telluride. “There’s about 30 seconds of it in our movie where we animate a couple of old photographs,” the Oscar winner said in a video interview from the Colorado festival. “Oh, and there’s some mice,” he added. “It’s very good for animals, and we had some mice that run around The Sun newsroom.” Some viewers of the movie took to social media this week to ponder whether AI had been used to reanimate old images of the Kray brothers and former UK Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher. Per Boyle’s video from Telluride, the answer to that would seem to be yes. Watch on Deadline Vanity Fair earlier asked Boyle what he thinks about the use of AI in film, to which he responded: “It doesn’t really matter what I think about AI. It matters what 20-year-olds think about it. My opinion of it is that it’s a very useful tool in many ways, provided you use it respectfully and provided you pay actors if you’re going to replace them with some kind of AI embodiment.” Earlier this week, speaking at the Venice press conference for Ink, Boyle had voiced concerns about the impact of AI on certain sectors, including journalism. “The danger with the tech giants and their AI is that they will be able to replace journalism. They’ll be able to have an AI journalist who’s much more efficient, cheaper, etcetera, ecetera, and will that AI journalist speak truth to the power that created it?” Ink, starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy, charts the rise of the UK’s notorious tabloid newspaper The Sun in the 1970s under the editorship of Larry Lamb, after he was poached from the Daily Mirror in 1969 by then budding media mogul Rupert Murdoch. The Studiocanal and Netflix film, which launches in December in cinemas and on Netflix in January, received largely positive notices out of Venice and currently counts an 85% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes.

entry.title: Natalie Portman Welcomes Third Child, First With Partner Tanguy Destable - The Hollywood Reporter
entry.body: Natalie Portman is now a mom of three. Portman, 45, welcomed her third baby, her first with partner Tanguy Destable, in Paris last month, according to People. The Hollywood Reporter reached out to Portman’s reps for comment but did not hear back. The Oscar winner announced in April that she was pregnant with her third child in an interview with Harper’s Bazaar, saying she felt “very grateful,” and that it was “such a privilege and a miracle” to be expecting a baby with Destable, a French music producer. “Tanguy and I are very excited,” she said at the time. “I grew up hearing about how hard it is to get pregnant. I have so many people I love who’ve had such a hard time with it that I want to be respectful around that as well,” the Black Swan star continued. “It’s such a beautiful, joyous thing, and it’s also not an easy thing. And so I know how lucky it is. I’m very aware, and I’m very grateful. I have deep appreciation.” Portman shares two children with her ex-husband, choreographer Benjamin Millepied. People previously reported that Portman and Destable’s romance was confirmed in March 2025. In her Harper’s Bazaar interview, Portman also reflected on the perspective she has gained with age and the gratitude she felt during her third pregnancy. “There is a gratitude that when you’re young, you don’t necessarily grasp,” she said. “There’s a calm and knowing myself: who I want to spend time with, what kind of energy I want around me that makes the experience so beautiful every day. And knowing it’s probably the last time, I cherish every moment.”

entry.title: Star Trek's Gene Roddenberry Tried To Kill A Major TNG Storyline Because Of One Character - TVLine
entry.body: Star Trek's Gene Roddenberry Tried To Kill A Major TNG Storyline Because Of One Character As the creator of "Star Trek," Gene Roddenberry was innately tapped into the plotlines that made up the greater universe of the franchise — but sometimes, he didn't exactly see the vision, like when he tried to kill a major storyline on "Star Trek: The Next Generation" over one character. Somehow, Roddenberry didn't see Worf, key Klingon Starfleet officer and Federation ambassador to Qo'noS, as a major character on TNG, so he — and nearly he alone — was against centering the show's Season 4 finale around the start of a Klingon civil war. "In Gene's mind, Worf was a character that he put on the bridge just to put into the background so that you could comment on the fact that the Klingons and the Federation were at peace now," executive producer Rick Berman told the episode's writer, Ronald D. Moore, during development, according to the book "The Fifty-Year Mission: The Next 25 Years," by Mark A. The creatives surrounding Roddenberry were not on his side. "I know we all see it differently," Berman added of Michael Dorn's character. Gene doesn't want to do a whole cliffhanger about him." Worf and the Klingon civil war changed Star Trek forever At the time, leaving the "Star Trek: The Next Generation" Season 4 finale on a cliffhanger in which Worf fled the Enterprise to fight in a Klingon civil war seemed like a well-rounded arc for a dedicated supporting character — one that the show's writers seemingly thought deserved creator Gene Roddenberry's blessing. How strongly Roddenberry felt about keeping Worf out of the Season 4 finale spotlight is unclear, because ultimately, he didn't get his way. Producer Rick Berman discussed the concept with Roddenberry following his pushback, and the creator ended up folding on the plot point. The decision changed Klingon history forever in the canon of "Star Trek," but the creative disagreement highlighted how out of touch Roddenberry had become — and how his influence over the canon had declined over the 30-plus years he had been shaping the franchise. Years later, the iconic character would prove his staying power and Worf would appear in "Star Trek: Picard" in 2023.
entry.summary: Star Trek's Gene Roddenberry Tried To Kill A Major TNG Storyline Because Of One Character TVLine

entry.title: RHOA's Phaedra Parks finally confirms new romance with 'Traitors' costar - USA Today
entry.body: RHOA's Phaedra Parks finally confirms new romance with 'Traitors' costar The "Real Housewives of Atlanta" star says her “castle daddy” is more than a friend – and she’ll be CT Tamburello’s date at the Creative Arts Emmys. It's a "Traitors" love story. "Real Housewives of Atlanta" veteran Phaedra Parks, 52, confirmed that she is dating "The Challenge" star CT Tamburello, 46, on a Sept. 4 episode of SiriusXM’s "Jeff Lewis Live." After host Jeff Lewis asked the attorney and legal analyst if her relationship with Tamburello was platonic, she kept her response short and sweet: "No, it's not." At first, she only confirmed she was seeing someone named "CT," before a radio listener phoned in to connect the dots and ask if it was her "castle daddy" from "The Traitors" Season 2, which she and Tamburello competed in. However, she decided to keep the details of their relationship minimal, only teasing, "I can't give this to you. I've gotta save it for the world." She later confirmed that she will be Tamburello's date to the Creative Arts Emmy Awards on Saturday, Sept. 5, where he will present an award alongside his "Challenge" costar Johnny "Bananas" Devenanzio, who also appeared on "Traitors." Elsewhere in the interview, the reality star revealed she has been seeing Tamburello romantically since around the time of her last appearance on "Jeff Lewis Live," which was on Aug. How did Phaedra Parks and CT Tamburello meet? However, the two's history goes back to Season 2 of the Emmy-winning reality competition series "The Traitors," which premiered in January 2024 and was filmed in Scotland in late 2023. In the murder mystery, Parks competed as a traitor working with "Big Brother" alum Dan Gheesling, "Survivor" alum Parvati Shallow and "Below Deck" alum Kate Chastain to deceive and "murder" the faithful. She made it to seventh place before being banished in the penultimate episode by the remaining faithful, which included Tamburello. "I'm voting for Phaedra," Tamburello said during Season 2 while banishing Parks at the roundtable. "I think you came here to be the opposite of who you are in real life, and I think you've been the best traitor we've seen yet." Tamburello and fellow "Challenge" alum Trishelle Cannatella became the first two faithful players to win "The Traitors" after successfully being the last two standing. Throughout the season, Parks and Tamburello interacted playfully, with Parks calling him her "castle daddy," prompting many fans to speculate they were flirting and others to make video edits shipping them on social media.
